utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. The Prosecution, I only notice the presence of Mr. McCloskey for the time being. And Defence teams, I think the situation unchanged, everyone is here, like yesterday. You, the Prosecution, has already taken six hours and fifty minutes, just for your information. I'm sure you know that. So let's start, unless you have any preliminaries, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and everyone. I want to begin in what will be a relatively brief presentation this morning, but I want to begin with some comments about the Borovcanin case, as per the directions of the Court. First, on their brief, I read it and found it to be detailed and thorough, for the most part articulately written, but fundamentally flawed. It was full of unreasonable conclusions, misstatements, and mis-analyses of the Prosecution's case. We absolutely stand by, as we always have, the legal proposition, if there are two reasonable interpretations of circumstantial evidence, one in favour of the Defence and one in favour of the Prosecution, the Court must go with the version in favour of the Defence, but when you look at this brief, you really need to examine carefully their analysis and look at their sources because they're not reasonable. They're articulate, they're intelligent, but they're not reasonable. I can't go through all of them. I'll go through a few. And there are some fundamental flaws in the way they're coming at this. One example. They criticise the Prosecution for concluding, in the opening statement, that -- or, excuse me, in the trial brief, that Borovcanin was in Potocari on the early afternoon of the 13th, and whether 3.00 p.m., 3.30 p.m., is early afternoon or mid-afternoon, and this is what they say on that point: On page 60, paragraph 90. Now, I got a corrigendum apparently last night at 10.30 that Ms. Stewart just put in front of me, so I'm hoping this isn't in their brief anymore, but this is what they said: "The Prosecution erroneously alleges in its pre-trial brief that this visit, the visit to Potocari, was in the early afternoon of 13 July, citing the Petrovic video images as its source. This may seem like a minor factual error, but it would be naive not to view this as part of a pattern of minor misstatements designed cumulatively to create an entirely false impression." The Prosecution is deliberately twisting facts to the Trial Chamber to create a false impression for you. Now, this kind of thing gets said. I usually call it false exuberance or over-exuberance, excuse me, but it's a theme throughout. They give an example in my opening statement; twist things, say something I never meant to say, and tell you it's part of this pattern. Another example of this I need to respond to is that in paragraph 163, they tell you that we withdrew two Sekovici witnesses, and they call into question our motives for this and suggest that our claims regarding why we did this are specious. And they go on to say this: "The Prosecution's deliberate strategy of not calling direct eye-witnesses should not be lightly excused. The question is: Why would the Prosecution do this? What tactical advantage do they hope to gain? What aspect of their testimony might prove inconvenient or exculpatory so as not to out-weigh the potential incriminatory value of the testimony? Is it safe to draw inferences based on the circumstantial evidence knowing the Prosecution deliberately chose not to present eye-witness evidence?" Paragraph 164: "Please see our filings on this matter filed 23 January 2009 and 16 February 2009." These witnesses had become under the authority of the Court, the state court. They had stood on their right to remain silent. First they were indicted, then they were acquitted. Mr. Thayer, myself, Mr. Vanderpuye, are licensed to practice law in the United States under the rules of our states in the District of Columbia. We are not, under those rules, allowed to use the force of process to call someone like this that is facing potential loss of their freedoms, and we stated as much; yet we're having this thrown back in your face and they want you to imply that it's part of this continuing theme of theirs. I hope we don't see it in the closing argument. It's unreasonable. We can handle it, but it shows their reasoning isn't -- is over the top, and we see that. Look at the way they've analysed the two Kravica warehouse witnesses. Completely off the mark, completely unfairly. And it's not just the Prosecution, as I said. They state three times in their brief at paragraph 89, 101 and 186, something along the lines that when Borovcanin is in Potocari after 3.30 p.m., the evacuation was essentially or effectively over. They say that three times in those three different paragraphs. And if we look at P02986, it may come up on the screen, I'll take you back to part of that video that was shot by Petrovic, which as we know, Borovcanin was right there. There's a huge line of separated men next to a huge line of buses. This -- he wasn't there for that long, under his own words, a half an hour, 30 minutes, and the time span seems to reflect that. So he's there during a crucial, crucial time-period, not when it's essentially over. They base that on the statement of van Duijn, who said something about the large group of people is no longer there. Well, remember the large groups, some 20.000, 30.000 people in a couple of photos. Well, that's true, but there's still a lot of work to be done. And that statement is just not reasonable, that it's essentially or effectively over. He's there during a critical period, separations, of the horror of what's going on, and he's got his cameraman with him who's editing out the various bits of horror that we know. In addition, I've got to go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As I want to just take you to one UNHCR document on this point. It's 5D01446 from a person that's reporting on Potocari. It gives us a very good indication of how late this evacuation is going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, interestingly, there's some very significant changes from the statement of Mr. Borovcanin, which I'm sure you've carefully gone over, the statements that he gave to me over -- two different statements with several days in between. He's a very bright, very capable police officer, commander, that came into this well prepared. This was not where he got picked up and suddenly talked to in an interrogation room. And as we've stated in the brief, he had a very well thought-out but flawed defence, that under his version, basically, freed him of military responsibility, and it went like this: That he learned -- he was ordered by General Mladic, in the early afternoon of 13 July -- excuse me, 12 July, right before anything is really happening, I believe, in terms of the bussing, to take his units to Zvornik; not towards Zvornik, to Zvornik. When he told me that in the interview, "to Zvornik," I asked him, Well, where in Zvornik? And he said, The Zvornik Brigade headquarters. You can see, as we cite in the brief, I was astounded by that because I knew that his units were stationed along the road. We'd had the first public version of the Petrovic video for a long time at that point, and I knew that the critical point that was needed at 12 July was that road, not Zvornik. But he continued to push that theme, and of course he acknowledged that he was along the road on the 13th and came up with the story that as he set off, it became dark, even though he said he set off at 4.00 p.m., and it was too dangerous for his troops, his Pragas, his tanks, to go up to Zvornik. They've been sending women and children along that route the entire day. The only dangerous -- really dangerous part of that route at that point was between Konjevic Polje and the Drinjaca River, a few kilometres that Borovcanin's army couldn't manage. Well, it was an absurd comment. And then he tried to explain that he -- so he got stuck and had to stay on the road. And then he said he got orders from the MUP, so now he's under the command of the MUP. And I said, Well, are you under the command of the army? And he goes, No. So he's not under the command of the army anymore. And then he comes, No, I am for combat purposes. So he's stuck in this terrible place he's gotten himself in. It makes no sense. However, he has now put himself with orders into Zvornik, saying that he's now left Dusko Jevic and his other units behind, no longer in command, and he's not working or doing anything with the army, he's stuck in limbo along the road. This was his defence. It's laid out perhaps more articulately in our brief. Well, now the brief comes completely off that, as far as I can tell, and is now repeating what we see in his reports on the matter; that he is ordered by Mladic to go to the road, and he takes his troop to the road, which means there's an acknowledgment, even though there's no evidence of it, that all of that material that he told me were lies. Well, they obviously were lies, so now they're agreeing. Unless they're not, we'll see, maybe the stories of -- of being too dangerous to go to Zvornik and being blocked and all that is still at play, but I don't think so. So this is a radical change, trying to make the story more reasonable. And at the same time, the story switches to, yes, he is issuing orders to Dusko Jevic to take part in the evacuation, which if you recall my interview, he doesn't want to have anything to do with Dusko Jevic after he leaves Potocari. That's Dusko Jevic, he's working with Momir Nikolic, I have nothing to do with them anymore. Now that's changed, after testimony in this case that's uncontroverted, no reason to lie. He's now acknowledging he's issuing orders to Dusko Jevic. There is no more indicia or indication of command than the issuing of orders. He stays in the Bratunac area on the 13th, the 14th, as does Dusko Jevic, both in Potocari, his troops, and along the road. There is no question he is in command of Dusko Jevic and his troops and in control of them. They make an amazing allegation, which Mr. Borovcanin never made to me. As a military man, I can't imagine him trying to tell me this, that, oh, yes, he was issuing orders, he was present in the area, but he was not exercising command or control over this unit. Nonsense. That would violate the rules, the law, common sense. It's completely unreasonable. We see him in Potocari on the 13th, when this awful stuff is happening, and his commanders are on the field, separating people. Also, as in his interview, when we got to the road, we were playing a video and asking him about who these men are, he's telling us, Oh, the people that are capturing the men, those are -- those are Milan Lukic's men, those are army that are taking the men and guarding them. My guys are on the road. We're not really involved. And then he makes this comment: "I cannot exclude the possibility that one or two or more of my men were involved." But he does not want to have anything to do with the capturing and the detaining or the dealing or the coordinating of those men in the interview. It's as clear as a bell. And now, at paragraph 166 of their brief, they're acknowledging that his men are taking part in the capturing and the detaining of these men. They even go on to say that his commander, Cuturic, who was -- coordinated with Momir Nikolic, who we know is also going up and down the road at this day, coordinating those captures and those detentions. So this is another radical change where they're looking to the common-sense view of the evidence and under-cutting significant parts of the statement of their client. It's an attempt to make it more reasonable. But, of course, how does that affect the overall package? It makes it less credible, the overall package less credible. And as we'll get to a little bit later, from the version that a Muslim soldier took a weapon, shot a Serb MUP person, the Serbs grab the gun away, burned his hands, and then fire back, which we agree happened - you can see that, as we said, in the brief from the health records, that happened - but Mr. Borovcanin's version is: After that, Milos Stupar reports to him that Milan Lukic's men fired back, committing mass killings. There's no suggestion of a two-part legitimate escape attempt that they're talking about now in they're brief and then a systematic murder happening later on that night. It doesn't get into that at all, and I'll tell you, and I'm sure you'll agree with me on that, the one person in this courtroom that knows what happened at the Kravica warehouse that night is Ljubomir Borovcanin, and he had the ability to tell me that -- or tell us that. He didn't. Had it been a legitimate escape attempt, he could have very well told me, and he should have. But now the story has changed, and I'll get into the support of that story a bit -- a bit further. Let me go to a couple of conclusions that the Defence make. Page 23, paragraph 41, they say: "Even if Borovcanin somehow surmised improper coercion was underway" - he's referring to Potocari - "his only viable course of action by that stage was to alleviate the humanitarian situation." Well, let me tell you what his viable options were, and this is important because I'm sure in our lifetime we're going to see international troops in this situation again, refugees coming in. The Geneva Conventions are clear. When you know a crime is afoot, and he must have known the intentions to toss those people out, he should not have been involved. When he heard about the assault to go into the enclave, he should not have been involved at all. If he'd walked away or refused, he wouldn't be here today. Now, as we've always said, part of this assault had a legitimate aspect, so let's give him the benefit of the doubt. Even though he knows what's going to happen when he gets there, that they've focused on this -- on the population and they're going to toss them, he takes part in going through the minefield and he takes control, with the VRS, of Potocari. That, by itself, still leaves him time to get out. Does he get out? No, he doesn't. He could, he did not. Now, once he found out and was aware that this -- and was ordered to take part in the separations and the forcible transfer of the population, it is not the Prosecution's position that he had to prevent -- try to prevent that. He did not have the military capacity to take on Mladic and Mladic's VRS. I don't expect that. I don't think the Geneva Conventions expect that, but what they do expect and what he knows by training is that he should not have been involved. He could have done what the ICRC did in Zepa and Srebrenica and just refused, just don't take part. He could have also done what the Dutch did. He could have helped the Dutch. He could have put a security cordon around to look after those people, those civilians, and maybe those nine guys wouldn't be dead and the 10th person that was shot up against the wall and the other horrors that happened wouldn't have occurred if he had helped van Duijn and Rutten and Koster, and made it clear to them, Hey, I don't agree with what's going on, I'll help you. At the very least, keep his men from separating people. You recall van Duijn. His men were separating people from the first moment of the -- on the 12th of July, and it went all the way to the 13th. Mendeljev Djuric was taking part in that. We've seen him on the video. The testimony was absolutely clear. He did not have to do that. And when he did, he was substantially assisting not only in the forcible transfer, but clearly, under any reasonable evaluation of this, by the end of the 13th of July he must have known that these men were going to be killed. And so by continuing to command his men in the process of the separation, he is substantially contributing to the murder operation. And follow the men that his men has separated. They go to Bratunac. He leaves them in Bratunac. He doesn't protect them ever, even though he knows of the murder operation on the 13th and after Kravica. Should he have disarmed the soldiers? Well, we don't have any beef with the idea of disarming the Dutch soldiers in the armed combat situation or as they're approaching. But once they're inside the confines of the area around Potocari and the Dutch soldiers are trying to protect these masses, and they're of no threat whatsoever to the Serb forces, there's only one real reason they're dismantling -- the Serbs are dismantling the Dutch, is to make their job to do the separation and forcible transfer easier. That's the problem here, not -- not taking their weapons pursuant to the assault. I have no major disagreement with that. He could have also gone up his chain, Goran Saric, his command, and said what was going on and reported it. He could have gone to Tomislav Kovac, the minister -- the assistant minister. Miroslav Deronjic, he could have gone to Deronjic, who had a connect with -- at this time with Karadzic. Deronjic recognised that there was no screening going on, that this was a wholesale grabbing of both men -- old men, boys, and able-bodied men, without any screening to determine whether or not they were war criminals or able-bodied. Deronjic even recognised that. Look at his testimony. He didn't go to any of those people. He should have done those things as a commander. The Geneva Conventions require them. They asked the question. I give you my answer. They also say: "The Prosecution has not shown that Borovcanin was animated by any other intent than to assist in the evacuation." Now, I won't reiterate all the involvement of this horrible process that he was involved in and the separations, but I will remind you, and you want to look at intent, look at his false statements to me, insisting that Jevtic were taken away from him, insisting that he was just visiting Potocari to take care of the bus situation on the 13th. His false statement saying he knows nothing about the separations, he's lying to me about that because he knows that these are all crimes that he is involved in and his men are involved in, and it shows a consciousness of guilt. That shows his intent. He also acknowledges now that he -- his units were working closely with Momir Nikolic, Radoslav Jankovic. Of course they are. They're doing the same thing. And, remember, we have a clear picture now that he's acknowledging he's taking part in the detentions and the capturing of the men in Sandici, because remember what's going on in Sandici; the same thing that's going on in Potocari. They're asking people to stand up, anybody born after a certain day, and they let those little kids, some of them, off and they allow them to get on the buses. So Borovcanin's unit and his people that he is fully aware of, because he's up and down that road, are separating, in this case, the kids. They're taking IDs. They're not taking any names. They're not giving them any food. They're not giving them any medical. Horrible things are going on, there are people that we see on stretchers. Remember the forensics. They found stretchers in Glogova. Do you think the people -- the Muslims who came out on stretchers were carried all the way to the Kravica warehouse? No, there's evidence in this case that shootings were going on and killings were going on in Sandici. So the same things that are going on in Potocari are going on in Sandici. He is under the command -- he is commanding the bulk of those units along the road. He's commanding a significant part of the units in Potocari. It's the same thing. He's trying to rely on this dog that will just not fight, that the security officers are commanding, the security officers are commanders, that Momir Nikolic and Radoslav Jankovic are commanding this thing. Well, I hope you can put this to rest. I will stand up for the accused's security officers on this point. The difference between their criminal responsibility and the responsibility of the commanders is immense. It's not even close. Our visceral -- reaction of the men that are organising the killings is visceral. It's like we hate those local drug dealers that are involved in the killings, but the Harvard grad that's bringing in the cocaine on his Lear jet is harder to get a handle on. His kids are in law school. So don't aggravate the case against the security officers. The real responsible guys for this are the commanders. Of course, the security officers have responsibility, but there's always going to be people to take the security officer's job. The commanders are the ones that are going to really have the ability to stop this, and don't buy into their argument. Okay. Now, Kravica, I want you to -- I don't want to play that body video again, but I do want to give you an exhibit that is a panoramic compilation so you can get a one-picture view of what Borovcanin and Petrovic saw as they drove by. I've given this to Borovcanin yesterday, and, Ms. Stewart, if you could pass out this to everyone, I think it's easier. It doesn't really come out very well on -- I don't -- well, it may come out on the video, but I would prefer that everyone just have this. You may or may not want to refer to it at various times. Now, in their brief and in their opening statement, they asked a couple of good questions to the Prosecution, a couple of questions that need to be answered, one of which is: Why on earth would Borovcanin take Petrovic around with him, filming Potocari, filming the road, and certainly filming Kravica? Why on earth would he do that, if he was actually part of this? Well, one of the answers is very simple. He received, as he told me, a written order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon has raised an important issue. Have you given a copy to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would trust that Defence counsel will have done that, but we have copies for the accused as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: He has a copy, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But all the accused should have it, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And thank you, Judge Kwon. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. So the question of why, why the journalist? Well, he told me in the interview, page 51 to 52, that he received a written order from Goran Saric to take Petrovic with him. Well, there's one reason. He's following orders. Also, we know from his stunt on the 12th in front of the cameras, propaganda was very important for the Serb cause. They needed heroes. They needed to report back that there were men in uniform doing their job for the cause, and so they needed journalists they could trust to shoot film they could trust that they could come back and play. Well, they trusted the wrong journalist, because we see, even before Petrovic gets involved, Borovcanin is handing out cigarettes to children, but we also see in the back petrified Muslim men, and it's part of an arrogance, a stupidity, as well as the propaganda effort. People committing crimes make mistakes. This was a stupid mistake on their part, to be doing this, as he fully understands now. And for why he would have taken him and not done something about it to the actual Kravica killings, well, having your men suddenly shot and killed by a Muslim, when your men are supposed to be doing the executing, that may make you forget immediately what exactly is going on as you rush down there to take care of the problem, and you have your trusted person, who is there, to edit out any issues. Well, there was a lot of editing going on in that movie. There are 24 seconds of the filmed shot at the end which should be, if you look at the testimony of Thomas Blaszczyk on this, there's 24 seconds of a black-out and other items played that should be that section right after the bus and the last little open room that gets cut, 22 -- 24 more seconds. I wait for the phone call that that material gets found. The second good question was: Why would Borovcanin, if he was guilty, bring the OTP the Petrovic film, the section that was played over Studio B? Well, the answer to that is: That was part of his overall strategy. He was betting that we had or we eventually would get that film. It was shown on public TV. You can see the advertisement for a Rolling Stone concert under it. It was the best strategy to bring it to us and try to put his spin on it. But then why does he -- why doesn't he tell us that this is an escape attempt, a legitimate escape attempt, that his men had to quell? We know it was his men that were involved, given with army and others. His men were there, his officer was there. There's very reliable hearsay in this case. Stupar, on 15 July, told the group at the meeting of the burned hand story and said his men, the MUP and army as well, fired back and killing everybody. It's very reliable hearsay, as well as the other second-hand evidence and other evidence that we've laid out in our brief. We don't discount that there were army there. Where there's one Red Beret, the special unit, there are other Red Berets. The Red Berets are the one disciplined unit in the Bratunac Brigade that would be expected to be at the executions. So this was part of a strategy. And he has come off, as we've said, that first statement to me as part of that strategy, to try to make it make more sense. It's a continuing effort, a continuing strategic way of avoiding his responsibility. Now, I've spoken briefly about Mr. Borovcanin and his control of the road on the 13th. That is in the brief. I think that is clear. Yes, there will be some army people at the Kravica warehouse. We don't find any army folks in Sandici or along the road, and the documents indicate this is a MUP operation. Borovcanin, his tanks, his two anti-aircraft, his mortar platoon, his soldiers from the various companies, they're the ones that are there, they're the ones that are in control, they're the ones that have the power over good and over evil. It's paragraph 189 where the Defence acknowledge that Cuturic would have coordinated with Momir Nikolic about the closing of the road. This also would allow us to infer that Momir Nikolic is coordinating with Borovcanin's people as well, not just the MUP in Konjevic Polje, which of course would be in close communication with Borovcanin's units. And recall the afternoon of the 13th, as we get closer to the warehouse situation, that Mladic and his senior officers are at the Sandici Meadow and for the first time really see the large number of prisoners that are there. This is after an organised execution, the Jadar River, a bus and an execution squad was used, where Cerska Valley likely started on the 13th with three buses, an excavator, and I'm sure the orders, if you look, came out at about that time that these men are to be killed. And that warehouse was right there, and they figured that out. So we have Borovcanin in control of the road, we have him coordinating with the army, we have Mladic and the group passing through. I think we can definitely infer they gave some orders. Let's see how far we can take this inference. You've got to look at everything that happened that day before you can make the inference. Well, as you know, Petrovic recorded the video, and we got snippets of the radio conversations that Borovcanin is having with his men, and one of them is stopping the traffic along the road. Now, if you evaluate that, that -- and you look at the time stamps, which the Defence agree are accurate, a time stamp appears at 1649, I believe, and then shortly thereafter is the order to -- for Cuturic to close the road. And when we add up the time shot in the video and the travel time and the cuts, he cannot have issued that order to close the road before about 1654. So it's after 1655, we believe between 1655 and 1700, he issues the order, Close the road behind your back. Now, we know that happened because Pepic, his officer, Pepic, says to Cuturic, his overseer, that he gets orders to close the road, and he does that. He's not great with times, but we clearly see -- we hear -- we hear the order and we see how it happens. And as you look back at this, when you evaluate it, you'll see that the Muslim men must have been in the warehouse or almost in the warehouse, giving the benefit of the doubt, when the order to close the road was made. And I'll get to how you can figure that out. It's in the brief, but this is -- this can be complicated. The other place where we can go to time is we know from the Bratunac Health Centre that the first soldier that's wounded in the "burned hands" incident, as we call it, gets to the health centre at 1730 hours, at 5.30 p.m. He gets shot through the arm, which can be a very dangerous -- unlike television, a shot through the arm with a high-velocity rifle can cut your artery and kill you in no time, so he is going to be -- we can infer fairly that after he is shot, he is going to be taken to that health centre as soon as possible. It's about a ten-minute hurried drive from Kravica to the health centre. So if he's checking in at the health centre at 5.30 p.m., his shooting incident, the "burned hands" incident, happened 10 minutes, maybe 15 minutes earlier, at 5.15, 5.20. And that's about the time Borovcanin arrives, shortly after that incident, 5.15, 5.20, thereabouts, because he hears it immediately. He's in Sandici, according to the video. He says he's a little bit farther away, but no matter what, he's going to be coming there as quick as possible, and there's no way to get him there, less than about three minutes, no matter how far he is. So he's getting there shortly after it happened; 5.15, 5.20, give or take. And when he gets there, we see this: Many bodies piled up. So we know something horrible has happened in the time between he closed the road and he arrives, and he had to have closed the road after 1654 and there's dead bodies at 5.15, 5.20, thereabouts, lots of them. Now, I had said before, I think in a question, that it was our position that the doors that you see on that warehouse were open and that the way the soldiers were acting meant that everyone in there was dead. Well, we have looked at some of the -- well, all of the conclusions in the Borovcanin brief, and not all of them were bunk. This particular conclusion of theirs, that these were closed doors, we carefully reviewed and we agree with. You'll see other -- if you look at this very carefully, you'll see other pictures shot through those open doors, and the windows in the back of the warehouse cast an eerily similar look as this photo. But we agree and I've offered to enter in agreement of facts for the record for you that these doors are closed, so we cannot now conclude, as easily as we could before, how many people are dead, except that group of 15, 20, 30, that we see scattered all the way from one side of this photo to the next. That's a lot. And as I read the Borovcanin brief, they fundamentally agree with our times. They leave a little more space, but they fundamentally agree that the shootings happened between 5.00 and 5.30, and it's necessary for their new defence that this was an escape attempt. So the question now -- the big question that we get to, when you can go through this and you listen to my colleague is: Is this all there is? Is this an escape attempt, or is it a full execution in process? Well, to answer that question, you go to the two survivors. They answer the question. It's why the -- and the Borovcanin team understands that. It's why they attacked the particular survivor, the one on the west side or, as they call it, the right side of the warehouse so vociferously, because under his testimony he goes into the warehouse, his group is the last group - the other side is already filled with the other survivor and his group - and the last man that comes in and packs that warehouse doesn't have a place to sit, and the Serbs open fire on him and open fire on everybody, and the shooting goes on and on and on until nightfall. Now, that is not an escape attempt, it's not at the "burned hands" incident. That is an organised and systematic execution. Now, what support do we have for that? Well, that's one -- Witness 157 -- excuse me, 156. Witness 111, who is at the other end of the warehouse, he is there, and then suddenly outside the warehouse he hears automatic gun-fire and all hell break loose. He's not exactly sure where it's coming from, but it's close by. He hears automatic weapon fire and crucially, crucially, he hears hand-grenades. You don't use hand-grenades to quell a "burned hands" escape attempt. When your soldiers are all around you, you're not going to pull a hand-grenade and toss it at the guy who's got the weapon. So if hand-grenades are used in the early part of this execution, as described by 111, it's a significant indication we have an organised execution. What other evidence do we have of hand-grenades? Well, Borovcanin, himself, in the interview tells us that when he hears over the radio that something terrible has happened, he hears detonations in the background, so -- and then when we see him on the Petrovic video walking around Sandici, this is after he has closed the road, listen -- listen to the tape. You can hear automatic weapon fire and explosions. This is shortly after he's closed the road. Celic, this Serbian MUP guy that's there, that sees the column walk by, also hears hand-grenades at this point. There's no hand-grenades used to quell some minor "burned hands" situation. The use of the hand-grenades and the other heavy weapons, look on that side of the warehouse, is a key -- an important and significant indication. Let me show you -- you may recall the Nicholson video which I believe is P01575. We've got an exhibit to show you. I don't want to show that whole video again, but I've got an exhibit that shows you where the hand-grenade release handles were found around the warehouse. Several of these handles were found outside the two back windows, so more indications of hand-grenades. We've just taken -- looking at this diagram, there was one grenade handle found at the end of the warehouse, right -- and then a group of six in front of the area of one window, and a group of four in front of the area of the other window. Now, I probably don't have the time to carefully go through the testimony of 156 and 111, but the only difference really of significance for your consideration is that after the shooting erupts, 156 says that it stops at nightfall, whereas 111 says it stops after a while, and then -- sorry. And then a half an hour later, firing erupts in his side. People come in and start shooting him, and that goes on and on and on, and he says it goes on intermittently through the night. And the big dispute here, they're theory that there's a systematic, organised execution that starts at night, is based on their evaluation that 111 is saying that this execution on his side happened as night was falling, at 8.30 or 9.00, because there is some indication that he's trying to figure that out, and he says night is falling, as far as he knows, and so that would be 8.30 or 9.00 at night. Well, to buy that theory, it's not reasonable because Witness 111 clearly says that a half an hour passed between the shooting that he heard on the other side of the warehouse and the time the shooting happened at his side. The question was asked: "How much time passed between those two events between the shooting outside and the shooting that took place when the soldier fired at you? "A. I think that in a previous statement I said that, but I will say that again. It's no problem. About half an hour passed between those two events." That's at 7060, 19 through 24. Then he says: "Firing in the east room took place intermittently. It was already dark, night had already fallen. And during the night, there was several breaks and then shooting would erupt again." Now, they're founding their whole view of this on his conclusion that he thinks it's 8.30 or 9.00 at night because he thinks it's getting dark. Well, you've been in that warehouse. Trying to judge what time of day it is based on light when you're inside that dark warehouse, is impossible. What he's absolutely clear on is that it -- that his executions happened a half an hour after the ones that happened next to him, and we know those happened about 5.00 to 5.30, when the lull occurred. So theirs is not reasonable. It's based on a guy that is feeling it's getting dark, and it may feel like it's getting dark, and they criticise 156. After gun-fire erupts and hand-grenades are thrown in, can you imagine, what can you hear? Hand-grenades go off that close to you, and other large weapon fire which there is evidence of, your head's going to be ringing like -- unbelievably. Who knows? Who could perform such an experiment? So his ability or memory on what he is hearing and when he is hearing it is going to be flawed after the shooting erupts. You've got to give him that; not so much for 111, where it hasn't started yet. He hears the hand-grenades, he hears the automatic weapon fire, and he also -- while that's happening, the soldiers on his side are getting agitated, which of course you'll get agitated if you knew you were participating and your colleagues were participating in a mass execution next to you. But then look at the testimony of 111, who they say is reliable. He does -- the guards say something, Ah, you see what your people are doing, suggesting that the Muslims are attacking and that's what the gun-fire is for. So look at all these things. It's the case within the case, and it takes very careful consideration. Most of it's in the brief on both sides. The Defence supports their version by citing the evidence of Mevludin Oric and two other MUP officers to say that there's evidence that it happened in the evening. Well, what happened is after the shooting erupted, Borovcanin is there, people are going to the health centre. Remember the testimony, Cuturic goes to the health centre, gets his hands bandaged up. Pepic eventually says he comes back from the health centre and reopens the road, and it's not Cuturic that's reopening the road, it's Borovcanin that's reopening the road. He's the one that's issuing the orders, of course, and controlling this. So within a time it's hard to determine precisely, but if you look at the time Cuturic goes to the health centre, he is checked in there at 5.40, so with the 10 minutes either way and the time it's going to take to get him dealt with, it's going to be at least an hour of him being looked after before he comes back and opens the road, and that's the time, a half an hour delay after Borovcanin arrives and they sort out their dead and their wounded. Then it begins again in 111's side of the warehouse, goes on for probably another half an hour, 40 minutes, and then that pretty much puts down the thousand people in the warehouse. Now, they're not all going to be dead, but they're going to be debilitated. The doors are closed on them. They're suffering. A high-velocity gun-shot in a crowded room with two to three people per square metre is going to be through multiple bodies. Constant firing of an automatic weapon is going to be able to kill and maim a lot of people. In some ways, it would have been better to torch the place. They would have died of smoke inhalation. Dying slowly of gun-shot wounds, bleeding to death, twitching on each other. This doesn't have to take very long. We have to ask you to think about that. None of us are experts. Well, some of us are. But this didn't have to happen, it didn't have to take very long. So by 7.00, we see the dead Red Beret, I think his name is Stanojevic. His body is taken to the health centre, so now we know the MUP has at least had time to clean up a bit. There's hay on the bodies that are in front. There's a bus in front. There's an old car in front of 111. They're able to close that place up. They need to do that to get the convoys running. And so after an hour, an hour and a half, roughly, of organised mass execution, this thing is bound up, and that's when Mevludin Oric and two MUP guys come along. They're not going to see anything. Yes, they hear gun-fire, there was intermittent gun-fire throughout the night, I'm sure on both sides of the warehouse, killing people as they moaned or stuck their head out or tried to get out or asked for water. We've seen that in all the other executions. The main difference -- well, let me go over 156's testimony. I'm sure Defence counsel will. He says, walking with the column, which we know happened, that he turns right, crosses into -- crosses in front of the warehouse. There is no fence, according to that witness. Then he walks between a bus and the warehouse. Look at the picture. There's a bus. That bus was not given to him. He drew that in on his own before he even knew there was such a photo. And that he walked through that door that's behind the bus in the photo, and over in the corner of the right-hand room near the river. And after that, he says he puts his head down, and we either don't ask him any more questions on that point or he doesn't remember anymore, but he does say that he goes out through the door he came in. And Mr. Ruez, when he was talking about the warehouse, talked briefly about that witness -- just a tiny bit of what that witness had told Mr. Ruez, when Mr. Ruez showed you the picture of the little guard room. And if we could show that picture to you briefly so you may recall it. Ms. Stewart can -- it should be P02103, if I'm correct. This is the guard room that Mr. Ruez talked briefly about, and he repeated a tiny snippet of what this witness had told him; basically, that the witness had managed to get into this room and protect himself from the firing. Now, we have the witness testifying that he goes in the far right-hand corner, and we have Mr. Ruez saying the witness told him he went into this room to protect himself from the firing. The fair inference from that -- and we have the witness saying he went out through that door when he finally got out, the one that you see on the photo. The fair inference you should make is that the witness managed to get across sometime after those executions or even -- he managed to get through his way as he's trying to get out of those doors and manages to get into that room and hide, not that he totally has two different stories, which will be the Defence version, I'm sure. And the fence, the fence is a big part of their brief when they discuss this witness. There was no fence. This witness clearly said, No fence. This is a -- I'll show you a brief blurb about that fence, if Ms. Stewart could hopefully -- you may remember Mr. Nicholson's video. This is the only way to get you to see this fence, and you need to take a look at it, because there clearly was a fence there in January of 1996, this little fence that they lean up against these older bars that were -- had been there a long time. But this is a little, weak fence that could have easily been kicked over to allow these hundreds of Muslims into the warehouse, and you can look at the Petrovic picture. There's no fence there, and that's when the witness is there. And we stand firmly behind the witness's recollection on that, and we'll show you the fence we're talking about so you can see it. Ms. Stewart can run the video, maybe still it on the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There it is. It's the shorter one of the two. That was in the winter-time pictures when Mr. Ruez was first there. This is April 1996. You will -- if you look in the exhibits, you'll see the winter-time, January. There's a shot of the fence, too. Unfortunately, it's impossible to conclude from these photos, whether or not Petrovic could have shot over the top of this fence, so that's why you don't see it in the video, or whether you don't see it in the video because it wasn't there. In any event, the witness is reliable. The fence could have been kicked over easily. There's no way they would have walked all this group around to come into this circuitous route when they can kick over a little fence. So those particular criticisms don't fly. Your Honours, that is a difficult subject. It's going to require patience to go through the material and double-check everything I said, double-check everything Mr. Gosnell said, but you don't use hand-grenades to quell a "burned hands" incident, and these two victims are reliable. They also attack, in their brief, the reliability of the witness who testifies about the execution of the men left over at Sandici Meadow. It's one witness. Why on earth would he tell of an execution involving his unit? The facts fit, there are extra people at night, it's Sandici. We find the same amount of people in a nearby grave. We can't prove beyond a reasonable doubt those people are the same as the ones he's talking about, but it's consistent. That execution would not have occurred without Borovcanin's approval and knowledge. Borovcanin has the conversation with General Krstic later on that evening, about 8.40. Everything's okay, no problem. I start questioning him about that. He runs from that conversation. Look at the brief about that. He is lying about that conversation and going back and forth on it, and it's an indication of consciousness of guilt, if I've ever seen any. He's in -- commanding those troops from the 14th. He doesn't go to Zvornik until the 15th. And look at what's going on on the 14th, too, the clean-up, the mess. It's still his units there. He's got to be held responsible for this. And, very briefly, he's in control of the road, he's got the men and the manpower. Yes, there are small elements of the army, certainly not Milan Lukic's guys. You recall in the intercept: Milan Lukic's guys on the 13th buses' broken down, and they're not around at the time that this is happening, and Beara two days later is really upset. So there's no Milan Lukic men, that's mystery men; that's blaming every bank robbery on Jesse James because he's the bad guy in town. Completely false. But, yes, there were Red Berets there, there would have been more than just one. There should have been Bratunac Brigade MPs. Momir Nikolic, who knows. When it comes to Kravica warehouse and Momir Nikolic, I have no idea. As Kweku Vanderpuye has said, corroborate everything Momir Nikolic says, but Momir Nikolic says one thing you can bet on. He was part of this thing. He knew all about it. He was coordinating with the MUP. He was all over the place. And now they're acknowledging they're working with these guys. So when Borovcanin understands what's going on here, he has got to stop it. He had the opportunity, when he came back to the warehouse, to stop it. He had the men. Unlike in Potocari the day before, he had the men and the material and the means to stop it. He didn't. The Geneva Conventions require him to stop it. He is guilty of 7(1) for not stopping it. Now, if I could, I'd like to go on to some brief remarks about General Pandurevic. If I could -- as you know, the brief was extensive on Pandurevic on both sides, and while I have the -- I have many criticisms of their brief, look at it carefully, their arguments are the arguments they've made from the beginning, that they made from the witness stand. There's no mysteries, no real last-minute curves. You've watched all that. You've seen it recently. You've seen me cross-examine General Pandurevic. I don't intend to take you through all that. There's no need to. But if I could get a break now, Mr. President, I could assemble my few remarks on General Pandurevic, and we'll come back and finish this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, your next target is General Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You can see the crew is getting ready to come in, and -- but if we could get a five- or ten-minute break after my remarks to get settled in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you have approximately, from what I'm told, about an hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. General Pandurevic. As I've said, you've seen the Prosecution and the Pandurevic case battle this out. I think the issues are clear, the documents are clear, the history is clear. I'll go over just a few of the points to help remind you of the Prosecution's case, respond to some of what the Defence has said. Briefly, the events of 1993, Operation Proboj, the conduct of the war from Directive 4, we were surprised to hear in the opening statements that General Pandurevic was going to be suggesting he was the hero of Kamenica. We still see that in the brief. But as you're aware, Directive 4 particularly says to get rid of the Muslim population, and perhaps a document that is second to none, in terms of its level of authority, was the order from General Zivanovic implementing Directive 4 in even more vicious language, to move out the populations of those areas. And Vinko Pandurevic was a key role -- had a key role in that. When we heard that he was the hero of Kamenica, we dug into the Drina Corps collections to prepare for cross-examination, and the deeper we dug, the more material we found. And you'll remember his reports, talking about attacking civilians and burning villages and cleaning up after mosques, reports that, in his particular bold style, got edited when they went up from the Drina Corps, cutting out that language. To suggest he's the hero of Kamenica, in my view, is appalling. The UN report, shells were dropping in on the civilians in the Konjevic Polje area, they're trying to get a hold of Pandurevic to stop that. It finally stops. That part of the history of the war is awful. He played a major role in it. That was abundantly clear. The attack on the enclave, he clearly played a major role. He was aware of the Drina Corps version of Directive 7 with the awful language in it. He's aware of the history. His group played a significant and substantial role in the take-down of the enclave. The 12 July meeting. The 12 July meeting in Bratunac, which he insists is on 11 July, frankly, I'm surprised that he insisted on that. I'm surprised that he continues to insist in that. In fact, in a document that we recently agreed would go into evidence, it was a statement of General Andric, saying he went to the meeting on the 11th, why the Defence wanted it in. But I'm asking him in that, Well, what was said at the meeting? Ah, well, it was on to Zepa. And I said, Well, what happened on the 12th? Well, is that when Mladic came and gave you the speech? Yes, it is. On to Zepa. Well, no one is contesting the fact that Mladic gave the speech at Viogor on the 13th, so Andric had it wrong by one day. I'd assumed in the beginning of this case that that mistake would be acknowledged, and even though it put them all in Bratunac on 12 July, the day the plan was first implemented in Potocari, I thought they would be able to suck that up. But their arrogance, unmitigated arrogance. The evidence and the intercepts, Jevdjevic, Bajagic and the stupid fish, they stuck to that story, these people, all the way through today to the brief? I know when you review the evidence that you know that meeting happened on the 12th. The intercept capped it. Why do they insist so much on that, I ask myself? It's because they're with Mladic. Dark things were spoken of. Why else would they go into that unholy trio of Jevdjevic, Bajagic, Pandurevic? The 13th of July, moves towards Zepa. 14th of July, is with the command, would have been able to communicate with General Krstic, who is fully engaged in the murder operation. The 15th of July I won't go into in detail. I've already done that with the morning of General Krstic. Remember Pandurevic's words to me about that. He, of course, had to know. He had to have been told what was facing his brigade when he went home. The amounts of resources involved in that required of it. If he was going to have any chance of defending his column from the Muslim from the rear, the 2nd Corps from the other side, the fact that there was a major murder operation in play at the time that Dragan Obrenovic has pled guilty for authorising and being involved in, had to have been mentioned. You must find that as part of your judgement. There is no other reasonable conclusion. Vinko Pandurevic by the morning of 15 July is fully informed, and he goes back to his brigade. He meets Obrenovic. Of course, Obrenovic tells him what's going on. He tells you, no, he learns it from some guy named Branko Grujic later on down the road. That is so patently absurd, it beggers belief. How does Eileen Gilleece get in her statement that he told Pandurevic about -- that Obrenovic told Pandurevic about it? She couldn't have made that up. She hardly knew the case. All the circumstances from the evidence, from his testimony and demeanour, again of course he was told about it. That yarn he spun was no more believable than pigs can fly. We'll talk about pigs a little later on. The 15 July interim daily combat report. You've heard me talk about it in detail in the opening statement. You saw us go over it in detail in the cross-examination. I don't intend to do that again. The report was written clearly. It meant what it said, its cryptic reference, its obvious meaning. The only other time I know Pandurevic to get that cryptic is when, on his 18 July report, he made reference to all the killings and how that it upset Zvornik and angered him. It's the same kind of thing. But in that 15 July report, he is taking responsibility. The additional burden for us, he is taking responsibility when he says that. He's asking for more troops, he's asking for people to come guard these people, come kill these people, and come bury them. He leaves out "kill" because that's too unseemly, but that's what he's asking for. He gets some help, but his units participate. And the brief on that is rather incomplete, incredibly incomplete. Look at our brief when you want to see the men, the materials, the units that are involved in this from the 14th to the 15th to the 16th to the 17th. And this defence that the Zvornik Brigade would have had to mobilise the schools in some official way, and therefore they're done by the civil -- it's absolutely absurd. Drago Nikolic and the MPs, of course, grab that school at Orahovac for a military purpose. It's under the authority of Dragan Obrenovic. When Vinko comes back in, it's under his authority. And they do that with all the schools. The fact that there's a civilian bulldozer driver that gets incorporated into the military operation, those arguments are so lacking in foundation I am, again, surprised they were even made. The argument that Beara came in and became commander, again, I've spoken about that. You've heard the experts on that. At one point in their brief, they agree with Butler, that a senior officer can come in and, of course, issue orders and people will follow them, but the first thing they'll do is tell their commander. But he cannot come in and take over command unless he's specifically designated to do so. Nobody's coming into Vinko Pandurevic's area of responsibility and taking over command. He would never allow that. That argument cannot fly. For this case and for history, that argument has to be put in the dustbin. Can I go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The 15th July report and Vinko Pandurevic's testimony provide a -- there is a unique window into the real meaning of that report, and it has to do with Eileen Gilleece report and the pigs. Now, Eileen Gilleece got some things wrong, but she got a lot right, and what she wrote was: "Pandurevic advised that Rick Butler refers to a handwritten report dated the 15th of July, 1992, at 2000 hours. That report refers to a pig farm near the 4th Battalion. The soldiers of the Muslim 28th Division seised the command post and killed pigs." Pandurevic acknowledges they had Butler's report. He now acknowledges that that had to do with "asanacija," though remember how this all started. Huge attack on Eileen Gilleece, a huge attack on "asanacija." "Asanacija" meant going out and looking for wounded or casualties first, and then, secondly, corpses and burial. But what we -- what he was explaining to Eileen Gilleece was the term "asanacija" in the 15 July report was a reference to when the 4th Battalion got overrun on the 15th and pigs were killed and had to be buried. That's what it says in the report. The problem with that is the 4th Battalion got overrun on the 16th, and it got -- or the late night of the 15th, after this report was written. That's the first problem. The second problem is there's no way on God's green earth a brigade commander, in the midst of facing what Vinko Pandurevic was facing, would report the burial of some 20 or 30, or whatever it was, pigs to the Drina Corps Command. Now, Vinko Pandurevic tried to sell that yarn to Eileen Gilleece, and she wrote it down. And in the direct testimony, something that was extremely well prepared and very well organised, and there was no more important topic in this trial than the 15 July daily combat -- interim combat report, look what Pandurevic said about that. He acknowledged, talking to Eileen Gilleece about "asanacija," but he noting, I'm sure, that she had mentioned in 1992 in her report, said that he was talking about an incident in 1992, in another area, 1992-1993, I believe, and that was the direct testimony. No mention of the seizing of the command post, as noted, and the 4th Battalion, and the Muslim 28th Division also noted by Eileen Gilleece. Completely left that out of his direct testimony. It had to have been on purpose. He does not want to get near that crazy story. So on cross-examination, General, what about the 4th Battalion? Go back and look at what he said. He tells me, Oh, yes, it did happen, and he throws in, Oh, there was an artillery barrage beforehand, trying to account for the fact that the pigs died before the post was seised. And he ends it by saying, oh, he told Eileen Gilleece both. Remember when I said, General, you've got to pick your pigs. He said he told her about the pigs in 1993 and he told her about the pigs in 1995. And if he told her about the pigs in 1995, just -- just like she said, so she's explaining "asanacija" with the pig story. It's absolutely absurd. It's a dead give-away. When you're caught up in a trap like this, it's hard to keep your lies straight, no matter how well organised and how good you are, and the attempt to cover every one with some artillery is what got him in trouble. He went way too far with that with Eileen Gilleece, he got in more trouble on direct examination, and in cross-examination he finished himself. He did that throughout on most topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you be specific as to the transcript pages, a reference? Look at line 8: "So on cross-examination, General, what about the 4th Battalion?" All I'm asking is for the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Vinko Pandurevic's testimony in direct examination that I referred to was 31286 to 31288. Pandurevic cross-examination about the 4th Battalion pig farm was at 32237 through 32240. And this is explained in the brief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That report means what it says. "Asanacija" means what it's always meant in this trial; the burial of the Muslims. "Obligations of security" meant guarding them. There's no question about that. And this document indicates Vinko Pandurevic took this burden on, as was his orders. Now, the 16th July, the hero of Baljkovica argued over how many of his men were killed. It depends on who you listen to. One of the colonels that went out and reported back to the Main Staff provided one number. Other reports provide others. It was a lot of men. If you add in the men that died in Srebrenica that are going to be adding on his mind on the 14th and 15th, he loses 20, 30, 40 men in Baljkovica, he stops it. That's why he stops it. That's clear in the evidence. He stopped it to save Serb lives. There's a suggestion that he did it to save Muslim lives. Well, there's no indication in this record that Vinko Pandurevic gave a hoot about Muslim lives. It was his job to kill the Muslim army. They had been killing him and his men. There's no indication that he cared about those Muslims. He opened that column to save his own men. That's why he didn't get in so much trouble afterward. The colonels went back and recorded he was in a tough spot. That's why he did it. This idea that he did it as some sort of a humanitarian gesture is just as absurd as being the hero of Kamenica. You got that feeling when he was testifying, when he talked about the Muslims and they were preventing any Serb life at a certain side of a river. There was no love lost there. Look at his morale reports and how he de-humanised the Muslims. Now, he does not care at that point about Muslim lives. He's trying to save Serb lives. The suggestion that he's the hero of Baljkovica is appalling. His 18 July report, where he indicates, you know, whose idea was it to bring 3.000 military-aged Turks, created unrest in Zvornik and problems for him, that showed he was angry and not happy that the Muslims were forced upon him and his town and the people. There's not one indication that it was the killing of them that was the problem. It was that he and his guys had to do it. He's complaining about the burden on him and Zvornik for having to do it, not that it had to be done. Did you get any remorse out of his testimony at all? I didn't see any. And there's not a shred of concern, or worry, or thought for the Muslims in any of his reports; certainly not those two, the 16th, the 18th, or the 15th. A report sent like that at his command to General Krstic would have been treasonous. Nobody is helping the Muslims, and that cannot be any more clearer than what happened to the Muslims after all this. The Milici patients linked directly to him through intercepts, and the fact he's commander and they're in his unit, severely wounded folks, yes, they would have seen the Muslims that were gathered in Nova Kasaba, the large amount of Muslims that have since disappeared, so the Main Staff, the Drina Corps, must have made the decision, Oh, we must kill the severely wounded people that are being held by the Drina Corps, so they send Popovic to go do it. He could have stopped that. He could have sent those people to Batkovic on his own, as he'd done many times before, I'm sure. He let them die. He let those four Muslim survivors of Branjevo Farm disappear the same way. He used them as witnesses against their own guys, who gave them sandwiches and told them where the front-line was going to go. He could have stopped that. He knew all about that. Who's responsible, who did this in the brigade? Three guys; Beara, Popovic, Nikolic? No, no. This took a unified effort of a brigade, outside units, the command structure, the security branch, the MPs. The Pandurevic brief, as I said, is wholly lacking in this. It's Vinko Pandurevic pointing down the line. It's awful. He has a hard time doing it, when it comes to Obrenovic. And remember the absurd, absurd suggestion that -- something about Obrenovic pled guilty, even though he wasn't guilty. That was his explanation for that. Absolutely crazy. He rather comes up with that kind of nonsense for you than put it all on Obrenovic. The commander at the time of the 4th Battalion, Lazar Ristic, was up to his eyeballs in this. He was at Orahovac. The commanders of the Petkovci Battalion, Marko Milosevic, Ostoja Stanisic, visits from Drago and Beara and had all those prisoners in their schools, there's much more to that story and their involvement. The Rocevic Battalion, Sreco Acimovic up to his eyeballs in this. When Vinko Pandurevic is back, his unit, his men involving in the executions, the transport, himself. There's no more important person for Vinko Pandurevic than the commanders of his battalions. These are the guys that command the guys in the trenches. If the guys in the trenches don't perform, Zvornik is lost. Sreco Acimovic is a key guy. Anything that Vinko Pandurevic needs to get done, he has to rely on Acimovic in that area. Acimovic is guilty, and Pandurevic isn't? The 1st Battalion, all their soldiers guarding people, helping in the transport, helping in the clean-up, working with the 10th Sabotage. They're responsible and Vinko Pandurevic isn't? Look at all the men and materials related to every one of those battalions, especially right after Vinko Pandurevic gets back, and you'll get a true picture of what went on and his responsibility. It's laid out very well in the brief. It's crucial for this Tribunal that the responsibility in this situation of a commander be understood and set out. Your responsibility in this regard is immense. Generations will be looking to your words. I'm sure you'll get it right. Now, in any murder prosecution, even a prosecutor has a hard time believing, many times, that the defendant committed the murder, that mothers kill their children, fathers kill their wives, fathers kill their kids, husbands kill their wives, so it's sometimes hard to get grips on, especially in mass murder. How can anybody do this? Do you have to be a demon or a devil? Well, the answer to that is no, and at this stage of the argument I'd begin to run out of words and I've tried to look to words of people that speak and write much better than I do. And in my readings, I came across a man that wrote something that I want you to hear, because it goes to this point. The man is named Leo Tolstoy. His words will be immortal, not because he writes brilliantly but -- that's one reason, but he clearly had his hand on the pulse of the human condition of war, of peace. I wish I was going to go to "Anna Karenina" with you, but I'm not. Of course, I'm going to "War and Peace." And in that story, there's a gentleman and an officer named Prince Andrew, and he's at the forward command post before a major battle with Napoleon. And his friend comes to the command post, his friend Pierre, and Pierre says to him: "'So you think we shall win tomorrow's battle?" "'Yes, yes,' answered Prince Andrew absently. 'One thing I would do, if I had the power,' he began again, 'I would not take prisoners. Why take prisoners? It's chivalry! The French have destroyed my home and are on their way to destroy Moscow, they have outraged and are outraging me every moment. They are my enemies. In my opinion they are all criminals. And so thinks Timokhin and the whole army. They should be executed! Since they are my foes they cannot be my friends, whatever may have been said at Tilsit.' "'Yes, yes,' says Pierre, 'I quite agree with you!'" It goes on: "'Not take prisoners,' Prince Andrew continued: 'That, by itself, would quite change the whole war and make it less cruel. As it is, we have played at war - that's what's vial. We play at magnanimity and all that stuff. Such magnanimity and sensibility are like the magnanimity and sensibility of a lady who faints when she sees a calf being killed. She's so kind hearted that she can't look at blood, but enjoys eating the calf served up with sauce. They talk to us of the rules of war, of chivalry, of flags of truce, of mercy to the unfortunate and so on. It's all rubbish. I saw chivalry and flags of truce in 1805. They humbugged us and we humbugged them. They plunder other people's houses, issue false paper, and, worst of all, they kill my children and my father, and then they talk of the rules of war and magnanimity to foes. Take no prisoners, but kill or be killed, he who comes to this as I have through the same sufferings.'" You don't have to be inhuman to feel like this in war, when you see your father killed, your family killed, and after three years of it, but it's a soldier's duty to deal with it. It's easy for me to stand up here and quote the Geneva Conventions. I understand that. I haven't been through what these guys have been through. But impunity, if we're going to stop it, this Court has to be the first line. Now, the victims in this case are never far from our minds. I always end with the victims. I don't trust my words. I've been doing this -- I have some words on my wall that I would like to take down, but before I do, I want to give them over to you. And my thoughts are always with those rows and rows of headstones at Potocari, and the eyes looking out at me from the video. And a soldier named John McCrae many years ago scratched down this poem in a place not far from here, and it's on my wall: "In Flanders Fields, the poppies blow between the crosses, row on row, that marks our place and in the sky, the larks still bravely singing fly, scarce heard amid the guns below. We are the dead. Short days ago, we lived, felt dawn, saw sunset glow, loved and were loved. And now we lie in Flanders Fields. Take up our quarrel with the foe. To you from failing hands we throw the torch, be yours to hold it high. If ye break faith with us who die, we shall not sleep, though poppies grow in Flanders Fields." This Trial Chamber is in the best position to give the men, the women, of Srebrenica some rest, some peace, some measure of justice. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. As agreed, we'll have a break now. Let me consult with my colleagues for how long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The decision is we'll have a 15-minute break now, and then, in the course of the question time, we'll have a further 15 minutes when we feel it is more appropriate. Okay, thank you. --- Break taken at 11.31 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll start from here: Mr. McCloskey, would you just state for the record who, as from your team, is present now, because I can't see everyone from behind the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Caitlin Chittenden, Chris Mitchell, Rupert Elderkin, Lada Soljan, Kweku Vanderpuye, Janet Stewart, and Nelson Thayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. As we said, we have a series of questions which we will put to you. If, for any of these questions, you need time to do homework, of course, you will tell us. We are not going to indicate to whom, in particular, any of the questions is directed. You choose who will answer the question. Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. To begin with, I have, Mr. McCloskey, some questions relating to crimes against humanity, in particular the "Chapeau" requirements for crimes against humanity. I'll begin with a very general question related to the attack, widespread and systematic -- or systematic attack. Now, yesterday Mr. Elderkin made reference to the Prosecution's position being that the attack on Srebrenica constitutes the widespread or systematic attack on the civilian population, and I presume that relates, similarly, to Zepa. What I'd like to know from you is: What is the Prosecution's position as to when that attack commenced? I'm not talking about the JCEs here, obviously. I'm talking solely about the "Chapeau" requirement and the Prosecution's position as to when the widespread or systematic attack on the civilian population began. And as Judge Agius has indicated, if in any of these questions you want to consider your position, you can certainly let us know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- the -- we had actually -- it's one of the legal issues we had discussed among ourselves and looked carefully into the Krstic judgement and the appeals judgement and their findings relating to that, but I cannot right now immediately recall. Whether we considered the attack - and I know "attack" doesn't mean necessarily firing bullets and artillery - whether or not we believe the attack starts with the squeezing and the formal start of the indictment from Directive 7 in March or we begin it with the actual operation. I would have to consult on that one, and -- but give me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our trial brief, at paragraph 2868, we talk a bit about this, where we say it's inconceivable that the very person engaged in the attacks upon Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves in July 1995 could not have been unaware that these widespread attacks were taking place. Indeed, evidence established that all the accused must have been aware of these attacks, owing to their intimate involvement in various and, in some cases, all aspects of the attacks, including, first: The restrictions of food and aid entering the enclaves; then sniping and shelling; further forcibly displacing. So that is the position. I couldn't recall, but we did start it with the restrictions as were formally placed, in our view, by Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: So Directive 7 is the starting point, is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. As we've set out, I think very clearly in the indictment, we're -- well, this business was going on for quite a while. Directive 7 is where we wanted to focus the Court's attention for the targeted charge of forcible transfer, the attack beginning with that pressure, and this sniping, and the restrictions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the second question also relates to this issue of the "Chapeau" requirements, and you have acknowledged and it's clear, and it's mentioned in several of the briefs, the point related to the column. I'm moving now to the column. You have acknowledged the military nature of the column, albeit with a civilian component to it, but the existence of the column as a military column, subject to military targeting. So my question is the relationship or the nexus between the military column and what you have alleged to be the attack, the attack on the civilian population. My question to you is: What is the nexus between that military column and the attack on Srebrenica, and is it a sufficient nexus to bring the actions against that column, the alleged crimes against the members of that column, within the concept of crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, let me try to clarify the position on the column. Many times, and I think I've been quoted in various briefs when I stand up in court and talk about that, and I, of course, stand by everything I've said, but many times the context of that is me acknowledging a particular reality, and I'm not necessarily making an overall statement. Usually, I get up and say, and I recall Judge Agius and I having a discussion on the record about this, is that the head of the column certainly was military and, as such, was a fair target, but we also see a tremendous number of unarmed and non-military men and boys within that column, even women we see. And there becomes a very grey area for us about when that can be attacked and when can't it be. And we have clearly a partial-armed column moving through the hills of Kravica. Then we have these people surrendering and getting blasted by anti-aircraft guns. That is clearly not, in our view, a fair target of the column, when people are being asked to surrender and are being blasted by anti-aircraft fire, even though that is the column. We've never chosen to charge that crime or that crime of perfidy in that case. We don't know who was killed up there, but it's not an absolute that this column was fair game and a fair military target. Parts of it were. It's in a grey area that we did not choose to go into as Prosecutors in the indictment, but because as that -- as the elements went through and broke through Serb lines, they clearly could be fought. Now, that group, with its military command, we believe, were part of the group that were forced out, out of fear of their lives. Now, this is similar to the Zepa situation, where only we have a retreating largely force of able-bodied men. They are victims in this case, in our view, even though they are part of a fleeing force. It's a mixed force. I don't think there's any question factually that this is a hugely mixed force. You get excellent pictures of this as they are coming out of Zvornik. There are a few guys with rifles and then there's this pathetic group of men, young and old, with no guns, so it's a mixed force, and these mixed guys with no guns that are no threat to the Serb forces are clearly, clearly, just as much victims of forcible transfer as the men that went to Potocari and got kicked out. The fact that they chose to run for their lives doesn't make a difference to us. The same thing with the military people. Yes, they are a target, but when the intent of the perpetrator in this case is to forcibly and permanently remove them, then they are also victims. It's a dual-motivation crime, something I've dealt with for many years in my home country; one good, one bad. If there is a bad motivation, a bad mens rea, you chase a guy out because he's a Muslim, because he's in Srebrenica, because you have this policy to make the Greater Serbia. You chase him out, even though he's a private with a rifle. You run him off your territory. You do that with the intent to permanently deprive him, even though that's not a requirement, but when it is permanently deprived, there can be no question he is a victim also, in our view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Okay. I think you've answered without answering what was to be my next question, which was whether the position of the Prosecution is that the column -- the members of the column were also the victims of forcible transfer. And I take it it is the Prosecution's position that the column and the members of the column, themselves, not just those who surrendered but the column and the members of the column, were part of the forcible transfer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. And if someone wants to get into the issues of au de combat and those issues it's going to have to be someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: No, that's -- for my purposes that's the point I wanted clarified.
