Now, I have some specific questions on this that you may wish to address or it was the area that Mr. Mitchell dealt with yesterday. These are specific related questions on forcible transfer related though specifically to the accused Nikolic, so I'm not sure -- I'll put the first question, which is in relation again to the forcible transfer. And I understood Mr. Mitchell's explanation yesterday as to the receiving of individuals who were forcibly transferred, those who had surrendered at the road, that the act of receiving or dealing with those who were received is what is being alleged by the Prosecution with reference to the forcible transfer and Mr. Nikolic. My question is: What evidence is the Prosecution pointing to to show knowledge on the part of Mr. Nikolic that these men, primarily surrendered, were forcibly transferred out of Srebrenica? What particular evidence would you direct us to on that question of knowledge? Because I assume you would acknowledge that the receiving of these individuals, for it to become part of the crime, would have to be with knowledge that they had been forcibly transferred. Simply accepting prisoners of war, for example, would not constitute a crime. So I'm asking for what the particular evidence is on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I can outline some of it. Perhaps Mr. Mitchell will help me with others. I would first point to Drago Nikolic's important position in Zvornik, which, as you know, was very closely connected to the Srebrenica enclave. They were involved in the restrictions of convoys. Sometimes convoys came into the area over the Zvornik bridge as opposed to always through Bratunac, and we see many of the convoy documents going through Zvornik. And I seem to recall Vinko Pandurevic saying that that's correct, that that was a Main Staff thing, We didn't have anything to do with it. But you'll see there's some Zvornik Brigade reports where they -- the one I recall is when they were taking medical sterilising equipment and other things that appeared to us they had no business taking at the Zvornik Brigade, and this was a process, as you'll recall, that was overseen by the security branch. And certainly in Bratunac, we have Momir Nikolic testifying about that, and I believe there's evidence that the security branch was overseeing the convoy entry and exit. That's normal, of course, because convoys are a security threat, potentially, smuggling, things like that, so it's only a natural part of security's job to know about that. So we can likely provide you with more evidence of the Zvornik convoy restriction, which should be in the brief section, and the security branch's knowledge of that convoy restriction, and then ask you to infer that that goes -- should contribute to Drago Nikolic's knowledge that the convoy is being restricted. Also, Directive 7 went to the Zvornik Brigade. The commander knew about it. These -- the history of the area was known to all the officers, and I think that is a very fair inference, that they know the history. The Zvornik Brigade was massively involved in pushing the people down to General Morillon, the enclaves being created, the convoy restriction. They knew that those people had run for their lives, that they were stuck there, and then he clearly would have known of the operation to take down the enclave. And he would have known generally -- remember Colonel Lasic, the guy that never made general, and you could tell why he never made general, is because he got up here and said something like, I knew what every VRS officer knew. We weren't -- you know, we're not going to live together, and that was the policy. Something to that effect. He knows it from the Drina Corps. Drago Nikolic has to know of the policy and practice to move out the population of Muslims from Eastern Bosnia. This was part and parcel to -- I mean, remember Vinko Pandurevic's morale documents. We have them, I think, April, May. He's -- it's rife with the idea of bringing back Serbia to Serbs and getting rid of the Muslims. This is the -- it's a propaganda calling card to rally the troops, and it's in many of Pandurevic's documents that have to go to Drago Nikolic and will go to Drago Nikolic, and he will absolutely know. This is something that helped give them hope and, you know, We're getting the enemy, including the women and children, out of our lives so that, you know, we can live by ourselves, and so genocide will not be perpetrated upon us again, like it was in World War II. This is the propaganda that was being fed to everyone, and with the results to back it up, that they all had to follow and take part in, from convoys to seeing some of the operations that went on. I'm sure Drago Nikolic would have been aware of some of the operations. The 10th Sabotage got together with the Bratunac Brigade, I think it was June of 1995, to go in and just to create havoc in the enclave. That is, given the connections, is something that he probably was aware of. But overall, his knowledge, he had been fully aware of the big picture. And the little picture, remember, 168 knew that there were at least 3.000 people that had surrendered on the 12th and 13th, and the phone call from Drago Nikolic directly related to prisoners, was clearly, you know, connected to the massive numbers of people that are surrendering. The Zvornik Brigade sends down -- has to send buses down there. This is something that he should have been aware of. It happened very visibly, it had a potential -- a potential threat to Zvornik. Zvornik troops were away at the time. Drago Nikolic, as the security officer, had to be very aware of what was going on down there because the word, as you could tell -- Obrenovic knew very soon that there were people heading up in his direction. This would have definitely engaged the security and intel forces. And so when you keep track of the army and the soldiers that are heading in your direction, you clearly know that there's civilians and the civilians are related to it, because they are completely interrelated. I want to just very briefly -- it's really impossible to separate the separation of men and setting them aside for execution and the forcible transfer of the women. The same troops are doing it. It's not, you know, one little group that's doing the separating and one little group that's doing -- they're all doing the same thing. They're using the same vehicles. They can't transport the men up to Zvornik until they get the women and -- until they get the vehicles for the women and children. Now, I don't want to go into my argument without an answer to a question which -- it does remind me of -- we've got to look at these things together. It's not separate. As Drago Nikolic is aware of the military threat, he will know the civilian connection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're saying that the same troops did it, but you refer to two joint criminal enterprises?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We chose two joint criminal enterprises to try to describe this God-awful crime, and we did it based on our knowledge and review of the law of joint criminal enterprise as it came out. And we -- we, frankly, did not feel we could charge everybody with the murder operation that was involved in the joint criminal enterprise. We do believe that there may have been people engaged in one that were not engaged in the other, or merely -- or, you know, to the point of making it worth a criminal prosecution. That was -- that was done on purpose to reflect the best way to charge individuals without over-charging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but going back to Judge Prost's question, with your indulgence, do I read you well? Are you saying that there was no way anyone on the ground there could have understood the attack on Srebrenica, the final attack on Srebrenica, as possibly excluding a forcible transfer of the entire population?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the people in the Officer Corps that were familiar with the practices and the policies, such as Drago Nikolic and the others, would have been fully aware. It's unbelievably noted in documents, and it's from the directives and orders, to the Krivaja 95, to other things. The officers would be aware that this final push was meant to be the final unburdening of the area of Muslims. That has to be known; not to every soldier and every farmer in the trench, but the officer corps of the Zvornik Brigade, under the leadership of Vinko Pandurevic, yes. These guys knew it, they were fully engaged in it. As we heard, Vinko Pandurevic didn't think they'd be able to do it because he thought UNPROFOR would get in their way. He was wrong about that. UNPROFOR backed off or UNPROFOR backed off because of hostages. But they were very much aware of those enclaves, they were very much aware of those Muslims, and not least of which because the Muslims were a thorn in their side, militarily. So this was a huge focus for the officers, the people especially in security and intel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Coming back to that issue -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would be the border-line that would distinguish those who would be responsible and those who are not responsible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For forcible transfer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, given the dual nature of the attack order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A soldier that takes part in an attack or part of the processes, with full knowledge that a principal objective of that attack was to move out the Muslims against their will, is responsible; private, sergeant, lieutenant on up. Now, practically, what I charge in this Tribunal, with our mandate, the mens rea is no different, but it depends on knowledge and level of involvement. I would say we'd have to have significant, substantial involvement -- significant or substantial, and I can't remember which. Anybody remember? I'll be in trouble with Mr. Kramer. But once they have significant and substantial involvement with the knowledge of the criminal event, and that their actions will result in that, they're part of it. There's even law that when they can -- you may infer that if situations where it's -- there's a reasonable likelihood that their conduct will result in that, you may infer that they intend the reasonable and likely consequences of their acts. I think that's even fair. In our case, that's not an issue. These people know what they're doing, and they know that their actions are causing the crime, forcible transfer or the murder. That's the intent I've spoke about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you exclude the possibility of a soldier or officer who would follow the attack order while not obeying the illegal part of that order, given that there's a legitimate part of that order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I just spoke briefly of Borovcanin on that point. He knows -- historically, he's very well aware of Bratunac's families there. He was the chief of police. He knows precisely what this was about. He received intelligence that civilians were there, that there were military-aged men there. He knew that they were going to go in and get rid of those people. He's given an order to attack. He knows that the troops who's he's under the command of are going to take part in that attack. He is a senior officer. I think he is guilty when he takes part in the attack. Now, you can tell from my closing argument he's part of the attack. I don't really seriously personally start getting any kind of a worry about him in that until he starts going into Potocari and taking part of the -- the physical movement of the people, and allowing the abuse, and doing the separations. That's where, personally, I hammer Borovcanin. His involvement in the attack, while I think is technically a violation because he knows it's criminal, he knows he cannot be involved and he knows he is involved, if you look even under the RS regulations, he's guilty, whether personally -- we would have charged him had he stopped and reversed out of Bratunac, I can tell you, we wouldn't have. But would he have been technically guilty? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could expand further why you think Mr. Pandurevic is guilty in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In that -- well, it's fundamentally the same. Vinko Pandurevic, as we have seen, he has pointed out, he was at the meeting in - was it 1993 - with Karadzic, he was in Boksanica in 1995 with Mladic. He was one of the premier officers of the VRS. He went on to be minister of defence. He's a published author. He was a significant force and a man and thinker at the time. He, better than anybody, knew the objectives. Look at those morale things. He knew the objective was to throw them out. He had been following Directive 4, following the orders. His knowledge was immense, his intent was immense. He was the one who issued those morale orders that glorified the moving of the Muslim population out of the area. So he knew precisely what this was about, and he is the kind of guy that has the ability to effect change and say, No, Trnovo is where -- you know, trying to suggest change. Now, his career would have been over, had he done that, but -- so he goes into this attack with incredible knowledge on what the results are going to be should they be victorious. Now, had Naser Oric been there, had NATO done a more effective bombing campaign, and had the UN forces been able to protect the Muslims, well, Vinko Pandurevic would have been sent packing along with General Krstic and the Muslims would still be there. But that's not the way it happened. And once the ball started rolling, and the victories started mounting up, and the massive population starts leaving, then it becomes no more grey area, Your Honour. Vinko Pandurevic is still there, he's still engaged in it, and it's not just him participating in that initial attack. The grey area of when I personally begin to see criminal conduct I can charge is when the attack is successful and the civilian population is being targeted, and the mortars are falling on the people on either side of the road as they're leaving. This is the 11th of July. Vinko's forces are still there, he's still around. He's telling Mladic, We've got to, you know, get the weapons up in the hill. The Muslims are still around. He's fully engaged. So that's when I have no problem putting the forcible transfer right into Mr. Pandurevic's lap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: But, Mr. McCloskey, just on that same point, just as Mr. Pandurevic is aware of -- on your description, is aware of the background and the forcible transfer issues, he's also very aware of the military purpose behind the attack on Srebrenica. So is it your position that he's to say, No, to the attack, he's to say, No, pressing the attack further, knowing that there's this dual purpose that you've described to the attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think the law can allow for a huge grey area here. I think commanders need to know what is against the law and what is not. When a person has such a clear object - an illegal object - as written down in Directive 4, as written down in Directive 7, as part of an entire war plan, when they see that that is happening, yes, when they start fully engaging their unit, they should say, No. And that is the incredible duty of the commander. He has to say, No, under the law here, under the Geneva Conventions, in my view. Now -- because it's his intent, it's his mens rea, his joining the joint criminal enterprise here, and he's -- all of that's happening. He's intending to do it, he's knowingly doing it, he's participating, and it's a substantial part of the operation. It can't be that, Oh, when things start to go bad, it gets criminal. I mean, how is a general to know when it's criminal and when it's not? It's criminal from the beginning. That's when they have to say, No. Now, had he taken part in this and stood down, or written reports condemning everything and refusing to have his people involved in it, and done -- and helped the UN and people, and been honest with us about when he was in Potocari and when he was in Bratunac, then that is a horse of a different colour. But when you have a policy like this, that's so clear from the get-go, I don't know in the next 20 years where we're going to see something that's so clear as this, the six strategic objectives, the Directive 4. This is such a massively horrendous thing. Please, and I'll say this briefly, don't underestimate the horror of ethnic cleansing. This is a policy of ethnic cleansing. Yes, it has a military aspect to it because of what the Muslims are doing, but this is just as much a part of the policy of ethnic cleansing as anything you'll see in this case. And ethnic cleansing is worse than lighting a building on fire full of people. It's lighting a war, lighting a country on fire. What they did in Kamenica and Srebrenica is a long end of a long series of horror, that was not necessary. It's not necessary in war to do what they did. And Srebrenica was the final culmination of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question which is related to what you have been saying and what you have been asked. Is it the Prosecution's position that the aims of Directive 7 and 7.1 or "/1" couldn't have been completely achieved by the Krivaja operation, Krivaja 95 operation, alone, but without the specific attack -- final attack on Srebrenica itself and the forcible transfer of the population?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure I completely understand. I think Krivaja 95 was not meant to be the final -- I want to say "final solution," but it was not meant to be the final -- the final objective or the final movement to make Directive 7 happen. It's -- in the wording of the Krivaja 95, it's clear it's creating the conditions to create the elimination of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One wonders perfectly well my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. So Krivaja 95 was there to create the conditions to be able to follow through and get rid of the Muslims, but just create the conditions. Pandurevic is concerned that the UN would stand firm would have meant that they couldn't have gone any further, and so Krivaja 95 was only -- was only Chapter 1 in what they hoped to achieve. Well, with Pandurevic's success, his military success, and remember, he knows the objective and he is fighting hard, then Krivaja 95 also says somewhere in it, you know, Be ready to take advantage of the situation and move forward, something like that. All military plans have that. And so on July 9th, Krivaja 95 becomes the possibility for the final objective. That's why it's so important. Tolimir is sending Karadzic's message that they've agreed with what must have been Mladic's proposal to the IKM, to Gvero, and to Krstic, a hugely important thing. They've changed from a Drina Corps plan to create the conditions for the elimination of the enclave to, We are now going forward, the enclaves are going to be eliminated. The UN is weak, the Muslims are weak. Full speed ahead. Krstic, Gvero, Pandurevic, Mladic, Miletic, they're all involved, and then it becomes massive. And then it's the final objective. But, no, Krivaja 95 didn't start out that way. It was -- it was meant to be the beginning, then to roll on to Gorazde, which they never managed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'll put a question to you in -- it has multiple questions in one, basically, but you need to focus on the principal part of it. Who do you consider, as regards genocide is concerned, who do you consider, for the purpose of the alleged crime of genocide, to be the targeted group? And I'm asking you or whoever will answer this question for the following reasons: that, for example, we heard yesterday Ms. Soljan referring to the Bosnian Muslims in Eastern Bosnia. Sometimes we've heard others, yesterday and the day before, but also throughout the proceedings of this trial, referring to the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica and Zepa as being the targeted group. Also, there seems to be some sort of incongruity in the indictment itself; for example, paragraph 30 of the indictment refers to the killings of Muslim men from Srebrenica; paragraph 26 refers to both female and male members of the Bosnian Muslim population of Srebrenica and Zepa; paragraph 33 refers to the entire Bosnian Muslim population of Eastern Bosnia. Basically, since this is one of the issues that we will have to determine for the purpose of the count charging genocide, we need to know exactly what your position is as to which or who was the targeted group for the purpose of the genocide charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we describe the group which is -- as you know, the Statute says the group in whole or in part. We are, of course, talking about a part. And the group is the Muslims of Eastern Bosnia, and those are defined as the Muslims of Srebrenica and Zepa, and should include Gorazde, but primarily Srebrenica and Zepa, though Gorazde is also part of Eastern Bosnia and they were also the focus of the ethnic cleansing campaign, as you've seen from the evidence. On to Gorazde, Gorazde's next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. In your brief, final brief, you deal with -- at some length with regard to the Trnovo killings and the involvement of the Skorpions unit. My question to you is: What evidence are you adducing, because it's not clear from the final brief itself, which allegedly -- what evidences are you adducing which would connect the Skorpions unit itself, which allegedly committed the killings in Trnovo, with any of the accused in the present case or, for that matter, to any other member of the alleged JCE?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, just to remind the Court, factually, the six or seven victims from Trnovo all went missing. I don't know if it was Potocari or the woods, but clearly they were just -- just like Orjem [phoen] Soljic or Mevludin Oric, they had been separated and, at some point within this July time-period, got shipped all the way across Bosnia to Trnovo. Now, we see Muslims getting turned over from Serbia, to Bratunac, and being shipped to Bisina on the -- is that the July 26th time-period, I think, 23rd, and we see Muslims going across the river in late July and with the Serb forces after that, but -- so these are Srebrenica victims that get arrested in the Drina Corps zone of responsibility, and I think you can infer they end up in Trnovo because buses or trucks are going back to Trnovo that were used in the forcible transfer operation or murder operation. I can't think of no other reason why you would send somebody all the way to Trnovo, except they had troops there ready to do it. You put the Muslims in the vehicles that are going back already and you send them to Trnovo. Well, that's across Drina Corps and other corps lines. It's -- that has to be managed by the Main Staff. You don't -- and it's not just six. They're not sending six people in a mini-van all the way across Bosnia. I think you can infer that this is a busload or a truckload of people, and they are being shipped there to scatter and hide this horrible crime. And so the logistics of doing that, the fuel, the vehicles, that all involves coordination from the level of the Main Staff in order to do it. Someone has to connect with the forces on the ground. Remember, that the forces on the ground in Trnovo are these joint forces of army and MUP. If you'll recall, Borovcanin was commanding such a force when he was shipped over to Srebrenica. He had the Skorpions under his command, and he was reporting on them, on the end of June and July, the Skorpion that came and the others. So someone had to contact either that MUP or the army. It was the army -- Borovcanin was working as per regs, he would have been working under the army, so someone would have had to go to the army in Trnovo. Now, whether that was the Sarajevo Romanija Corps people, or it would have had to have been at the corps level. That would have to go down through the army command to the MUP command, because the Skorpions wouldn't be able to do any orders until their MUP guy, their equivalent of Borovcanin, whoever he was at the time, they would have had to go through him to be able to get him to engage these guys. So, yes, we have to make some inferences, but you don't get Srebrenica victims transported, with the fuel and the vehicles, and given to a very well-organised, disciplined Serbian unit, without massive communication and organisation at the highest levels. That's inferencing, but you just -- you cannot get across the country without fuel, without vehicles, and the approval to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you pointing your finger to any of the accused, in particular, or to all those who took part in this particular joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, for Trnovo, I'm not pointing at these accused. I'm not going to point at the accused for executions like that unless I've got evidence of the fuel, of the -- more something. I'm going to want some hands-on evidence before that. I can tell you that it would be almost unimaginable for the chief of operations not to know that they were shipping large numbers of Muslims across the country to be murdered. His involvement, his actual awareness in it, is too fuzzy to point any fingers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You're not alleging that the Skorpions unit was part of the Zvornik Brigade or under its responsibility, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll ask you a couple of questions on reburials, and then I'll give an opportunity to my colleagues, and then I'll come back to you later. Within the context -- Mr. McCloskey, within the context of the Tribunal's Statute, the law, and the indictment, is it your position that reburial, itself, constitutes a crime and that it's being charged as such, a crime punishable pursuant to our Statute, in other words? That's why I mentioned initially the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: By itself, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, it has to be done with the knowledge of what the purpose is and in furtherance of that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that was the question. Somebody who didn't participate in killing before genocide, not at all, participate in reburial, it is your case he's responsible for genocide, for killing, for whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we do believe that the JCE continues through the end of the reburial, and if you brought an officer in to make sure -- let's say they brought some guy from Serbia because someone else was busy, they brought in a specialist from Serbia to make sure that these burials went according to plan and were part of -- and really done it quietly. That would be a -- that would be a substantial contribution to it, and I think the issue would be a sentencing issue under our law. Now, we're talking about soldiers and bulldozer drivers and things like that. No. But if an officer comes in and is really providing a substantial and significant part to keep this quiet -- you see, murder, you've got to cover up. At home, it's not -- cases all the time, you've got to keep it covered up and keep it covered up. Mass murder is even more important, so burials and reburials and mass murder has to be viewed differently than we look at things domestically. So if someone comes in and provides some substantial assistance to something that important, to keeping this from the international community and keeping this crime quiet, yes, I would say that would be add -- be a substantial and significant contribution. We sometimes get a bit spoiled here. With a couple of less survivors and without aerial imagery, we may not have known anything. They could have been fully successful in this. The amount of luck and the -- it was the international community getting into Bosnia in January that allowed this to happen at all. And so the ability to come in and keep things quiet, be it Afghanistan, Iraq, the United States, or anywhere else, is a big deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, always on the subject of reburials, I've got a few more questions. You seem, if we understand you well, to be charging reburial as a natural and foreseeable consequence of the murder operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you expand on how you consider that reburials legally can qualify as a natural and foreseeable consequence, in the circumstances of the case? I mean, people like the ones you've charged, Nikolic, Pandurevic, Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, fundamentally, I view it in two ways: One, as any murder, you have to dispose of the body if you want to get away with it. I mean, that is a typical part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- of any kind of a normal murder, and it's absolutely foreseeable that the police or somebody are going to be able to figure out where you hid the body, especially when you have to act quickly, in the eyes of neighbours, or the international community in this context, and that it's absolutely foreseeable that you might have to move the body. Now, I take my neighbourhood murder example, but it's even more important on an international mass execution level. It's got to be -- Mass Executions 101 has to be where to rebury the bodies when the internationals figure out where they are, and how to do it. In fact, we taught them. In Kosovo, they didn't do mass graves anymore. They killed people and left them lying and stuck guns under them because of what they learned from Srebrenica, in my view. So it's absolutely foreseeable that people might find where you buried mass bodies, and they might -- and that you need to have a plan ready to do something about it, especially near the end of the war. You know, they -- that's -- in my view, that's foreseeable, that you have to hide the body from the authorities if they get close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You also charge -- yes, yes, Judge Stole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: Just on that one same question: The timeline is quite different when it comes to the reburials, compared to the burials, naturally, so the reburials would, in time, be quite a bit further away from the killings and the burials. These do not, in the Prosecution opinion, make any difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, it could. As you know, the burials took place from -- from 14 July through 17, 18, 20 July, the initial burials, and the reburials started -- well, the fuel started -- we see the fuel coming in, I believe it's September 15th from the Main Staff, so we have a few months. That's not very long, in my view. It's a couple of months. The longer the reburials were from the actual crime would -- it would depend on the circumstances, but the circumstances in this case are pretty clear. In July, there's no thought of -- immediate thought of Dayton. Well, the end of the war is considered near. That's one of the reasons why they want to push towards Srebrenica. The idea of NATO forces or people like that on the ground is really unthinkable, and that's one of the reasons why you see them acting so arrogantly and that documents can be written the way they are written, and only get found with search warrants. And so early on, in July, it was not a major concern, even though it should have been. But August, September, Madeleine Albright and her photographs in front of the UN, showing disturbed earth, that is all pretty quickly happening, and so it's after Madeleine Albright, who's in August, I believe, that in September we actually see the fuel getting there. So it's, you know, burials in July, UN photos to the world in August, reburials in September, boom, boom, boom. No big delay, no change of personnel, no other reason to be doing this. This idea that they had to bury -- rebury people for hygienic reasons, no. So I fundamentally agree with you have to look at the timeline and you have to see how connected it is, but in this case very connected. As I just mentioned, that's the outline of -- burials in July, the world knows in August, the fuel comes in September, and the bodies start dribbling through Bratunac and Zvornik in September and October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. McCloskey, just one more question on this -- from me, anyway, on this particular topic. This whole question of foreseeability, I want to make sure I understand you completely. In your argument that the reburial is particularly, and Mr. Elderkin argued this yesterday, a contribution, it doesn't really matter, then, on your position whether it was foreseeable or not; at the end of the day, it's another factor going into the contribution. And foreseeability, which sometimes can bring into confusion that there's some allegation of JCE 3 here, which is what I was not clear on, my understanding, though, after Mr. Elderkin spoke yesterday was that, at the end of the day, the foreseeability factor is really not that significant on your argument of contribution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin is absolutely correct, and we put a lot of thought into his argument, as did he, and that's what we came up with, and that's why that was specifically mentioned by him. JCE 3 and foreseeability is another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I have your point now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since you have mentioned JCE 3, I have a question about particularly the extended form of joint criminal enterprise. You charged the accused for opportunistic killing pursuant to that form of responsibility. The requirements for that is not only that it was foreseeable, but also that the accused took the risk willingly. So if you could explain to me what evidence we have as to whether or not and how the accused willingly took that risk. I'm particularly interested in knowing with respect to Generals Gvero and Miletic, because they were not charged for any killing, except for these opportunistic killings, while others were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, General Miletic and Gvero, while noted as members of the joint criminal enterprise to kill people, were not charged, and the foreseeable -- the opportunistic killings were specifically connected to the foreseeability -- to the forcible transfer charges related to Generals Gvero and Miletic, and so that's a -- that's a separate issue. And if I get your question right, it's the -- it's their willful and intentional involvement and substantial assistance in the ethnic cleansing of Srebrenica that provides the foundation of their -- that makes them responsible for the foreseeable actions, when there's no question in my mind that Generals Gvero and Miletic are fully versed in the horrors of ethnic cleansing. They see it. It's not only from the Muslims, as they're driving the Muslims out pursuant to these directives. They see it happening to Serbs. Grahovo and Glamoc. If we start this Tribunal over again, I would love to go to Grahovo and Glamoc and see what happened there, but -- so they see ethnic cleansing from both sides and they see how horrible it is. They see what happens when -- Western Slavonia, for example, we see what happens when the Muslim forces go in to clear out an area and what they do to some of the Serbs. So they see it from both sides. They know precisely what this means and how ugly it is. It's more than foreseeable; it's a surety, that soldiers seeking revenge are going to act out. Look at General Gvero's order of the 13th. He is actually telling his soldiers that, This Muslim column is going through and among them are inveterate criminals and villains, and you must stop them at all costs. You know, you might as well say, They're going to rape your children and wives. This is what, you know, the soldiers on the ground are getting fed, that the Muslims are coming to commit genocide on you. This is the bile that General Gvero is selling. He knows that when some Muslim is getting captured by Serb soldiers who have lost family members and have been given this steady diet of bile, they're going to act out. It's more than foreseeability, it's a surety. But certainly Miletic and Gvero, who have seen the ethnic cleansing and the results of it can foresee and did foresee that the ethnic cleansing policy would result in deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was not any foreseeability; whether they took the risk. But I think that your answer would do. But at the beginning of your response, you said that Generals Gvero and Miletic were noted as members of the joint criminal enterprise to kill people. Could you draw my attention to that passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's an annex -- I think it's an annex in the indictment where we -- as you know, I think, the law requires us to list those that we feel are in a joint criminal enterprise to kill people, and we listed them in there. It is paragraph -- paragraph 97, and we didn't do it without evidence to support it. We have not argued it, we have not pushed it specifically, because we didn't charge it. But when required to put down who was in it, we put it down. And I can highlight the evidence of their involvement, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I have a final question on reburials, and it's more of a clarification that we require from you than anything else. In the indictment, you specifically charge Accused Nikolic, Pandurevic, and Popovic with -- in relation to reburials, with regard to reburials. In your pre-trial brief, and for the record it's para 302 thereof, you seem to add Beara. And we've, in the course of the proceedings, heard submissions particularly from Mr. Ostojic on that. In the final brief, paras 1079 and 2282 and 2283, you once more mention Beara as being involved in the reburial operation. Incidentally, you also allege, in your final brief, that the VRS Main Staff coordinated the reburial operation with Miletic's knowledge. My question is: What is exactly your position as regards reburials, vis-a-vis both Accused Beara and Accused Miletic? Have they been put sufficiently on notice that ultimately they were going to be brought into this overall picture when they were not as such -- included, as such, in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I remember discussing this with Mr. Ostojic, and some evidentiary matters related to it, and I would need a small break to go back and see where we are on that because there may have been some changes or something. I need to -- let me look into that. General Miletic, we would have -- chief of operations has to know about something like this, and has to be involved in it, and know fully that it's happening. I mean, that's what that would be about. And if I can get back to you on Beara and maybe discuss it with Mr. Ostojic, I think we can sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just direct the Prosecution's attention to the November 8th and 9th transcript where we had a discussion in what I thought was a ruling from the Court, specifically on the 9th of November, 2006, where we had that discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the reason why we have brought this up, because the subject is returned to in the final brief. So, okay. Mr. McCloskey, Accused Nikolic and Gvero, in the final briefs respectively, make the point that the protection provided by the Geneva Convention 4 can only be applied to civilians, intimating at the same time that prisoners of war and detainees, whose detention is justified, cannot be considered as victims of forcible transfer or deportation. I don't recall this point having been touched upon in the course of the various interventions. Perhaps if you could deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I -- that issue, I think, was dealt with in the Vukovar case. There were some Trial Chamber rulings about those victims, and the holdings that come out of the Appeals Chamber, I think, are important here, and I would have to refer that to my colleagues for a discussion to become updated on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it you will deal with this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. While we are at that, Judge Prost is drawing my attention to another issue that we meant to raise that perhaps you can include with this one and come back to us at a later stage. That's the duty to protect prisoners, particularly within the context of the Mrksic standard, as contrasted with the Blaskic considerations. Yes. Borovcanin argues that the Mrksic standard can only be described as aiding and abetting by omission, and should not be used as the Prosecution has unmistakenly pleaded, Blaskic liability in respect of the duty to protect prisoners; that is, the intentional omission, direct intent which is intentional. Perhaps you can deal with this item now or later, but we meant to raise it now as worthy of some feedback from your team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Borovcanin brief says that we did not charge aiding and abetting for forcible transfer, and when I read it we checked the indictment. Everything is being charged with aiding and abetting. It's very clear in the -- in the indictment. I think they're -- they're suggesting that this particular form that we've chosen, Mrksic form, the Geneva Conventions, but the Defence -- I think the Defence expert referred to it as the duty to protect, I don't understand why they don't think we've charged aiding and abetting on that as well. However, I have assigned Mr. Vanderpuye to deal with that issue, and I'm sure he's prepared to deal with it, especially if you give him a moment or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you prefer to deal with it now or subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President, and good afternoon to you. I am prepared to deal with it now to some extent. The problem is I'm not entirely clear on what the Defence position is on it. But to the extent that I can assist the Trial Chamber with our position, I can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: What I'm particularly interested in, Mr. Vanderpuye, and I'm sorry, I can see you only on the video screen, is: Is the Prosecution alleging aiding and abetting by omission, the Mrksic standard? I'm particularly interested in knowing whether that is an allegation that the Prosecution is pursuing on the facts in relation to Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can answer that simply. This indictment was made, you know, obviously before Mrksic, and we intended and wrote "aiding and abetting" on each and every one of the Statutes and forms of liability. That's the way it was meant to be pled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And so what you're saying is that would include any aspects of aiding and abetting that have been developed in the law, even if they are developed subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely, and that -- that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For my purposes, at least, it's clear enough. But since this was a question that we had agreed to put together, are you satisfied with this explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. McCloskey or whoever, we have had a submission from Borovcanin, in his final brief, that as from 9th July 1995, UNPROFOR soldiers are to be considered as combatants for the purposes of the law. There are some allegations from others that that could have been the position even before the 9th of July, but let's stick to this Borovcanin submission. What's your position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure how fully relevant that is, but as I mentioned in my argument, I don't have a fundamental disagreement with it. The -- as they mentioned, there was the green order, and on, you know, the days leading up to -- and on the 11th, there was some -- some very minor resistance from DutchBat, and NATO got in the game and dropped some bombs. So to that degree, UNPROFOR was a potential target, especially if attacking or perceived to be attacking the Serbs. I have no problem with Vinko Pandurevic going in to a UN OP that's firing on him and taking away their weapons. I don't have a problem even if they're not firing upon him, if they come into the OP and taking away their weapons so that they don't get shot in the back by a Dutch soldier. I have no problem with that. Now, as I mentioned, once the hostility is over, and we're at the 12th of July, and the Dutch are sitting in their compound and standing around trying to look after the Muslim population and themselves, Mendeljev Djuric and his unit of deserters systematically disarming van Duijn's people and pointing guns at them and taking away their ability to protect the Muslims that they're in charge of protecting and themselves, now, that's another matter. That is done with the intent to move forward the joint criminal enterprise to get at the population, either to separate and kill them or to move them out, and that's the conduct that I focus on. The other conduct related to what's going on with the OPs and NATO, we're not charging anything like that, and I don't -- I don't see -- it makes good reading, but I don't see how relevant it is, and I don't really object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, could my client be excused, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could my client be excused, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. Shall we continue, Mr. Josse, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I want to be very sure that I'm clear on the Prosecution's position on this. It's obviously a very significant point, and you spoke about it this morning, and it's obviously referenced several times in the brief. It's the issue of the command of the Zvornik Brigade's involvement, in terms of the participation of various aspects of the Zvornik Brigade in the course of the process with the prisoners and the executions. Is it the Prosecution's position that first Obrenovic and then Mr. Pandurevic specifically knew and authorised the participation, for example, of the various battalions that you made reference to this morning, or is it your position that more vague -- if I could say, that it fell within their authority, that there was general command/authorisation for participation, and then the battalions fell in line, if you wish, behind that general authority? Are you alleging specific knowledge and authorisation for the participation of the various units, other than the ones on which obviously we have direct evidence on, but the other extensive participation as you described it, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's no question in my mind that Vinko Pandurevic and Obrenovic were aware that the command elements of the battalions in the areas where these prisoners were held were involved. They would have known that, they would have had to have known that. The particulars of the movements and how it all went, not necessarily. The actual -- what Sreco Acimovic was doing, perhaps not. But Vinko Pandurevic would have had to know. He needed the members of Acimovic's unit. He had to have known that Acimovic was involved in this horrible, massive thing that was taking him away from his duties at the front. He would have had to have known that Acimovic, personally, and that his units, generally, were engaged in that operation. He had to so he could know how many he could bring to his front, how many he could ask for, what kind of demands he could ask from Acimovic. The same thing with the 1st Battalion up in Pilica. You know they -- there's lots in the record about the people in Pilica, because they were a bit off the combat track. They were constantly being used to go other places, and Pandurevic had to know that there was a significant number of prisoners that were having to be dealt with. When he says, The additional burden for us is the obligation of security for the people in the schools, he knows that the people in the schools are the obligations of his soldiers to guard. That's what's happening on the 15th. Twenty, thirty soldiers of the 1st Battalion, when he writes that, are guarding people at the Kula school, and there are people at Rocevic. The MPs, we've proven, are at Rocevic on the 15th, and the various units and soldiers of the Rocevic Battalion involved in the killing. He has to know all of that. This is why he writes this thing on the 15th, because it's a -- it's a burden and it's a total irritant to him on what he needs to do, and that's defend his lines and defend Zvornik. He has to know that. The absolute particulars of an involvement, he never needs to know absolute particulars, but he's the kind of guy that's going to need to know the details, he needs to know what his commanders are doing and that they're getting the job done, and he's going to demand that. He's at the forward command post, he's fully involved in communication with people, and he will know that his units are involved. And that is a massive distraction from him and what he really needs to be doing, and he has to know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: So then there's a quote or a statement that's attributed. A couple of times it's mentioned in the Prosecution's brief, attributed to Dragan Jokic, where he says: "The error of Popovic and Nikolic were doing what they wanted, taking whomever they wanted, wherever they wanted." That suggests, of course, the other position, which is that the security officers were carrying out these activities with the battalions without the authorisation of the Command. I take it, then, it's the Prosecution's position that that's not a correct statement of what was happening, because I don't think you can have it both ways, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I wish Mr. Jokic would have been more helpful, but from Mr. Jokic's perspective, who is a civilian -- civil engineer at the same time as a career officer, he's a weak character that when Beara comes into his office and starts saying, I need this and I need that, and Popovic is there also, and Drago Nikolic is, and they're all saying, I have orders from my commander, da-da-da-da-da-da, they're not coming in and doing things without the orders of their commander. What I would point you to, as we've done it before, is: In Zvornik the first thing, you know, Drago Nikolic does is he calls his commander. Before he can do anything, he calls Dragan Obrenovic and seeks his authority. Even Beara can't come in. Beara is armed with Mladic's orders, but even Beara can't come in and say, I have orders from Mladic, give me this. He couldn't get troops from Blagojevic or Nastic or the others. He had to call Krstic, General Krstic, please get these guys to give me troops. The security branch is having to go to the Command in order to get what they need. They can't do anything on their own. All the people, and the logistics, and the units that they need to get this massive job done are under the command of their -- of the commanders, and the commanders have to be involved in that at that scale. Yes, a very small scale, a -- Beara could come in and order this and maybe take a prisoner out and, you know, have him shot, and the commander could conceivably not know about it, but 5.000 people in the schools in a process from 13, 14, 15, 16, and 15 and 16 in particular for General Pandurevic, involving the massive aspects of -- look at our brief. I didn't have time to go over it. From the logistics and the fuel and the battalions, the amount of energy and resources that went into this, there's no way these three guys could begin to do that. Momir Nikolic reported to his boss, Drago Nikolic reported to his boss. Popovic, as Mr. Vanderpuye put it, reported to his boss several times, and Beara was getting called by his people, 155, several times during all this and is having to report back, and they're calling him. These are the command nodes running their security branch. This is not the security branch running the other way around. That is the tail wagging the dog, and it's just historically fundamentally impossible on this scale, it can't be done. They can't come in and just take what they want and do what they want at that scale. There's only three of them. They need the military police who are under the command of their commander. They need the units, the drivers, the other folks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I have your point. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see if I could run through these. I have got some minor question. Miletic final brief, page 9, para 16. There is a statement there that General Milovanovic, himself, acknowledges that in the spring of 1995, and in any case from March to late May 1995, he was at Crna Rijeka with the consequence that, therefore, no one could have stood as Chief of Staff or as deputy Chief of Staff, et cetera. Do you accept that part of the evidence, that Milovanovic was in Crna Rijeka particularly from March to late May 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd have to check with Mr. Thayer. I do remember what should be in evidence is the collection of reports to the Supreme Command. I believe we got in a huge collection of those throughout 1995, and some of them showed -- a few of them showed it went out under the name of Milovanovic during periods of 1995, and many others went under Miletic's name. And we think that's primary evidence of who's around. But there's more to it than that, and Mr. Thayer is familiar with that, and again I think if you give him a little bit of time, he can give you a more prepared answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The same final brief, pages 85 and 86, paragraph 213, the Miletic Defence team makes the point that the Trial Chamber had taken judicial notice that: "The Bosnian Serbs deliberately tried to limit access to the enclave by international aid convoys by early 1995, and fewer supply convoys were making it through the Srebrenica enclave, and, finally, that blocking aid convoys was part of the plan." This is what we are supposed to have taken judicial notice of. It is then submitted, basically, that the correct wording -- exact wording is that the Defence was, therefore, at a disadvantage, as the onus was on the Defence to adduce rebuttal evidence, which to me means that this judicial notice basically led to an inversion or a reversal of the onus of proof. Do you wish to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's clear that the adjudicated facts are something that does form a presumption, but it's a rebuttable presumption which Ms. Fauveau and General Miletic were fully capable of doing, and it doesn't -- and they would have done it, of course, anyway, in regard to our case. If the Prosecution had stood on that alone, they might have some kind of a concern, but if we had stood on it alone and they'd rebutted it, it would be over. So the fact that they have to rebut it, yes, that does shift the traditional burden to some degree, I think. I may get corrected by that statement, but I think practically it does. But as we know, an adjudicated fact sits there, it's not -- it's not something that you're going to -- when -- if something is hotly contested, I think everyone has faith that you're going to make your judgement on each side's case and not worry about your own adjudicated fact three years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 124, para 286 of the Miletic final brief, it reads as follows: "When an accused is alleged to have participated in a JCE, the nature of his participation must be specified, including the facts from which such an inference may be drawn." And there is a reference to some jurisprudence there. Then the same final brief continues: "At no point did the Prosecution allege that General Miletic contributed or participated in the restriction of UNPROFOR logistical supplies. This cannot be put down to lack of precision in the indictment, but to an omission which cannot be remedied by the evidence presented." So, basically, this is attacking the integrity of the indictment as it relates to Miletic. This is why I'm putting it to you, in case you wish to make any comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That is an issue that Mr. Thayer and I have discussed, and if we could put that on his list, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Ostojic, I think, is ready to answer the rest of our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leave Mr. Ostojic alone. Let sleeping dogs lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I just want to correct the record. On page 74, lines 19 through 22, it mentions that I said "May 8th," but it's actually the 8th and 9th of November 2006, and particularly I found that November 9th, the transcript at page 3876. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that deals with Miletic. Borovcanin. I'm reading, because otherwise no one would be able to follow, from paragraph 136: "The combat with the column, which the Prosecution in any event concedes was a lawful military target, was not conducted by the MUP alone, as claimed by Vasic in his dispatches. Vasic, for whatever reason, was apparently exaggerating the situation to his superiors." And then it continues, and this is the more relevant part: "Third, not all the MUP forces were under Borovcanin's command. The 2nd, 5th, 6th Zvornik PJP companies and the 2nd Deserters Unit were subject to a different chain of command and were not subordinated to Borovcanin under order 64/95." Borovcanin takes -- suggests or believes that the Prosecution has never suggested otherwise. Is he correct in this; in other words, that you have never suggested that the 2nd, 5th, 6th Zvornik PJP companies and the 2nd Deserters Unit were subject to a different chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure we've dealt with it, Mr. President, because the units that were specifically in the area of Sandici, in Kravica, and located in Potocari, are very clearly defined in the case, and these other units are -- go from more of the Lol ici towards Konjevic Polje area and are coming in at different times, and we haven't dealt with it. But I can tell you, under the Rules, and under the conditions and knowledge of this case, it's -- it's impossible to think that they're going to be bringing in PJP -- special police or PJP units working alongside Borovcanin units that are under the command of someone else. It can't work that way, it's not designed to work that way. Borovcanin is an impressive guy. He can handle these MUP units. They're not going to give MUP units in the same area as Borovcanin to some army commander or some competing MUP unit. So though I don't find it super significant, but the position of the Prosecution is very likely he's under the command -- that he's commanding any of these units, if not more than likely. I would say he is. Now, I need to correct myself on the -- on one answer I gave when I said I had no objection to the disarming UNPROFOR in the various operations. As I'm thinking about that, this is again the problem of the dual motivation. When Vinko Pandurevic dismantles UNPROFOR with the purpose to get at the civilian population, that is a contribution to the crime. When he dismantles UNPROFOR because they're firing at him, that's not a problem. When you have both at the same time, it is a problem. He shouldn't be doing it in the first place because it's a crime to go into a United Nations safe area to drive out the population. It's a crime to go into anywhere to drive out the population. And if you take out any force to do it, as a substantial part of making that happen, that's a crime. It doesn't sound good, we don't like it, but that's the case. This is a horrible crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When he, himself, has a dual motivation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And the higher you get up in the ranks, the clearer it becomes. The lower the soldier -- the soldier that's being ordered to attack the OP or the lieutenant that's going up there, you know, is one thing, but the people at the top of the food-chain like this, that know from the very get-go the horror that's involved and what's going to happen, it shouldn't be happening, and when they do it, going after UNPROFOR, be it Gvero, be it Pandurevic, Miletic, that, in my view, is a substantial contribution to the JCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I had some other questions which I'm going to skip because, more or less, they have been even marginally -- although marginally dealt with earlier. Again, Borovcanin final brief, page 176, paragraph 277, I'm reading: "Butler's view was that Vasic had no knowledge of the killing plan when he wrote a particular passage to which the previous parts of that paragraph refers, and that he generally believed that those men would be released as an inducement for the column of the 28th Division to surrender." If -- the question that Borovcanin Defence team put is the following: If the killing plan was not obvious to Vasic, who had been privy to the two main meetings held by General Mladic, then how could it have been obvious to someone else who had been out in the field and not involved in any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's probably best to have that report in front of you, but Vasic writes that report based on the 10.00 a.m., 12 July meeting at the Hotel Fontana, where Mladic is saying, you know, to the Muslims, You survive or disappear. And what Vasic reports shortly thereafter probably -- I don't know, I can't -- he didn't have times on his reports, but it's probably shortly thereafter, a few hours, on the 12th of July, is that Mladic -- in his view, Mladic is holding these people as a hostage to try to bring the men out of -- out of the woods. I don't know where he got that from, be it Mladic or not, but, yes, in our view, Vasic at that point has not been told of the plan. And by that afternoon, 12.00, you know, 12.00, 1.00, the bussing separations hasn't -- it's beginning to get going, but it hasn't really got going yet, and so the real obvious -- what's going to be clear to everyone is this lack of screening and this horrible abuse and these separations. This is where those that are not on the inner circle are going to start to become aware. Remember, on the 12th of July Tolimir, from -- where is he, outside of Zepa -- writes a proposal, which is his job, and says something to the effect, You know, make sure we gets lists of these people so we can get down -- so the war criminals don't get away. This means Tolimir doesn't know about it. He's in Zepa. He has not been told, because you don't get lists, and -- you know, that's what you do for exchange, that's the first thing you do, and that's what Tolimir wants, so that they don't exchange all these people without figuring out who the bad guys are. That's his job as security officer. So in the afternoon of the 12th, that's what he's writing. So Tolimir isn't in on it. There's an intercept. The same thing. It's on the 12th or 13th, where someone is saying, Hey, they're getting large numbers of Muslims. We've, you know, got to get in there; otherwise, they're going to get away scot-free. And the guy at the other end says basically, Don't worry about it. So somebody on the other end thought that these Muslims that were getting collected in Nova Kasaba were -- were going to be sent away. So the 12th of July, if you're not in on the inner circle, you're not going to know, but when you start separating people and treating them less than like as you would an animal, then the word spreads. The commanders that are doing it have to know what they're doing, because they have a duty to look after these people, to make these lists, to get them ready for exchange so they can get their Serb brothers back, and the commanders, like Borovcanin, that realise, We're not doing that, they're going to know why. So the fact that Vasic, in the afternoon of the 12th of July, doesn't know, it's not until the -- the separations and, you know, he's being engaged and he's communicating with the MUP in Bratunac, that he's going to be fully aware. As Miroslav Deronjic, you know, basically said, when he saw that there was no real screening, he knew something was up. So that's the explanation to that particular part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And last question for today, and it is strictly legal: I refer you to para 399 on page 225 of the Borovcanin final brief, and then to paras 411, 412 and 413, which you will find on pages 231 and 232. Basically, in the first of these paragraphs, the Borovcanin Defence team is stating that taking the wording of paragraph 30.4.1 of the indictment, they are understanding that paragraph as properly charging only superior responsibility, and exclude that the paragraph properly charges Borovcanin with having committed the act described in that paragraph, whether directly or by way of JCE. If his contention is not correct, then he attacks the same paragraph by way of alleging that he was given lack of adequate notice of what he was being charged upon. Similarly, in the paragraphs -- in the other paragraphs that I mentioned in pages 231 and 232, he is offering a blanket objection to Counts 3 to 6 and 8, alleging that they are vague, more or less mounting the same way of reasoning as in the case of the paragraph -- paragraph 34 or 81 that I mentioned before, and suggesting that the indictment, in his regard, does not charge aiding and abetting, except insofar as the Kravica warehouse events are concerned; in other words, alleging that aiding and abetting is not being charged in respect of any of the crimes committed in Potocari, and that includes the forcible transfer and other forms of persecution. I consider this allegation as warranting some kind of feedback from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We will do that. I can answer it briefly. It's ludicrous. I looked at his allegations, that we weren't charging aiding and abetting. We charged aiding and abetting for all forms. So we'll look into the particulars of that, and -- but I think we need to be careful here. Unless there's something that they can point out to that occurred at trial, or some other issue, the time for challenging the indictment is long past. If they're going to challenge the indictment on these grounds, that requires all accused to get up and challenge the indictment on this -- on those grounds. This is one of the clearest, most detailed indictments in this Tribunal, and we've gone through this entire process, and so unless there is some specific connection to the case that he can point to, it's -- the process is disconcerting. But we will absolutely answer your questions and be prepared to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can stop for today. I did have some more questions, but I think I will take the opportunity over the weekend to go through them again and see whether they need to be put or not. In any case, on Monday we will start with you, Mr. Zivanovic. We'll start with you after, of course, we've heard the final response from the Prosecution for the questions that we have postponed. Thank you, and have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
